statement: Agents that may access very large tool libraries should discover and load tool definitions on demand instead of putting every definition in context at startup.
A multi-server MCP setup can spend tens of thousands of tokens on tool definitions before the user task begins, and very large setups can reach six-figure token overhead.
Large tool libraries create accuracy risks beyond token cost, including wrong tool selection and incorrect parameters when multiple tools have similar names.
Deferred tool loading should keep only critical or frequently used tools visible initially while making the rest searchable.
condition: when an application has many available tools but a smaller set is commonly needed immediately

statement: A tool search mechanism should return matching tool references and expand only the relevant definitions into model context after search.
condition: when deferred tools are available through a searchable registry

statement: Deferred tools can preserve prompt-cache efficiency because they are excluded from the initial prompt and added only after search.
condition: when deferred definitions are not part of the initial prompt

statement: Internal testing reported substantial context reduction and improved MCP-evaluation accuracy after enabling tool search for large tool libraries.
Tool search is most useful when definitions consume more than about ten thousand tokens, selection errors are occurring, multiple MCP servers are connected, or ten or more tools are available.
condition: when the context or accuracy gains outweigh the added search step

statement: Tool search is less useful for compact libraries, libraries under roughly ten tools, or sessions where nearly every tool is used frequently.
exception: when the tool set is small, compact, or broadly needed in every session

statement: Tool names and descriptions should be clear and capability-specific because search quality depends on the indexed names and descriptions.
condition: when tools are discovered through text search over names and descriptions

statement: Systems using tool search should give the model concise guidance about the broad tool domains available so it knows when to search.
condition: when many deferred capabilities are not directly visible in context

statement: For large or multi-step tool workflows, the model should be able to orchestrate tool calls from code instead of performing every invocation as a separate natural-language tool call.
condition: when the workflow has enough scale or control flow to justify code execution overhead

statement: Natural-language tool calling can pollute model context because intermediate outputs are returned to the model even when only an aggregate or summary is needed.
condition: when tool outputs are large or mostly intermediate

statement: Natural-language tool calling adds latency and error risk in complex workflows because each call requires another inference pass and manual synthesis of returned data.
condition: when workflows require several dependent calls and result comparisons

statement: Programmatic tool calling should keep raw intermediate results inside the code-execution environment and return only the final, task-relevant output to the model.
condition: when intermediate results are not directly needed for model reasoning

statement: Code is a better representation for orchestration logic that needs loops, conditionals, transformations, parallel operations, or explicit error handling.
condition: when tool workflow logic is algorithmic or repetitive

statement: Internal tests reported lower average token use and better benchmark accuracy for complex research or knowledge-retrieval tasks using programmatic tool calling.
condition: when applied to complex tasks similar to those tested internally

statement: To enable programmatic tool calling, a system must expose code execution and explicitly opt individual tools into being callable from that execution environment.
condition: when tools are safe and intended for code-driven invocation

statement: Tools called from code should have results processed in the code-execution environment, with the model receiving only the code execution result when the script completes.
condition: when using the described programmatic calling flow

statement: Programmatic tool calling is most useful for large datasets, three-or-more-step dependent workflows, filtering or transforming tool results, avoiding irrelevant intermediate influence, or parallel checks across many items.
condition: when the efficiency or control-flow benefits exceed the overhead of code execution

statement: Programmatic tool calling is less useful for simple one-tool calls, quick lookups with small responses, or tasks where the model should inspect every intermediate result.
exception: when the workflow is simple, small, or requires model-level reasoning over all intermediate outputs

statement: Tool definitions intended for programmatic use should document return formats clearly so the model can write reliable parsing and aggregation code.
condition: when the model will consume tool outputs through generated code

statement: Tools that can run independently in parallel or are safe to retry are especially good candidates for programmatic orchestration.
condition: when selecting which tools to opt into code-driven calling

statement: JSON Schema defines structural validity but does not capture many usage conventions, such as optional-field inclusion patterns, correlated parameters, or domain-specific formats.
condition: when schemas are used alone to describe complex tools

statement: Tool definitions should include concrete input examples when correct usage depends on conventions or parameter combinations that the schema cannot express.
condition: when examples can clarify meaningful ambiguity in tool use

statement: Tool use examples can teach expected formats, nested object patterns, and optional-parameter correlations by showing representative calls.
condition: when the examples cover the relevant usage variants

statement: Internal testing reported a large accuracy gain on complex parameter handling after adding tool use examples.
condition: when tool calls involve complex parameter handling similar to the test setting

statement: Tool use examples are most useful for complex nested structures, tools with many meaningful optional parameters, domain-specific conventions, or similar tools that need disambiguation.
condition: when the accuracy improvement is worth the added definition tokens

statement: Tool use examples are less useful for simple single-parameter tools, standard formats the model already understands, or constraints that JSON Schema can enforce directly.
exception: when examples would add tokens without clarifying meaningful ambiguity

statement: Examples should use realistic data, cover minimal, partial, and full usage patterns, stay concise, and focus on ambiguity rather than restating obvious schema constraints.
condition: when authoring input examples for tool definitions

statement: Advanced tool-use features should be layered according to the current bottleneck: tool discovery for definition bloat, programmatic calling for intermediate-result bloat, and examples for parameter accuracy.
condition: when designing an agent system with multiple possible tool-use bottlenecks

statement: Tool search, programmatic tool calling, and tool use examples are complementary because they address discovery, execution efficiency, and invocation correctness respectively.
condition: when the system has bottlenecks in more than one of those areas

statement: A practical tool-search configuration should keep roughly three to five heavily used tools loaded and defer the rest.
condition: when there is a small stable set of frequent tools plus a larger long-tail library

statement: Future optimization of MCP-based agents should target schema orchestration and transport efficiency rather than tool execution speed.
Across every measured MCP deployment configuration, actual tool execution constitutes a negligible fraction of total token and latency cost.
condition: under lightweight-to-moderate tools
exception: production deployments with heavy I/O such as databases, remote services, or long-running computation may exhibit different characteristics

statement: In topologies with customized MCP clients, LLM planning plus schema injection consume 56-72% of total tokens and 60-67% of total latency.
condition: customized-client topologies (L-Cust and C-Cust)

statement: With an off-the-shelf MCP client (Claude Desktop), final answer synthesis becomes the dominant cost, exceeding 75-85% of total latency.
condition: off-the-shelf client topology (C-OTS)

statement: Deployment choices fundamentally reshape how computational effort is distributed across an MCP workflow, so the dominant bottleneck depends on the topology.

Profiling an MCP workflow requires measuring both token cost and latency, because MCP can inflate token usage through schema and tool-result injection and inflate time through additional protocol hops, and these effects vary independently across settings.
MCP standardizes how LLM hosts, clients, and tool servers communicate, reducing the n-by-m integration problem so tools can be added, swapped, or updated without re-engineering the whole agent stack.
Prior MCP benchmarks measure task success, grounding, and robustness but treat the protocol as an end-to-end black box, leaving protocol-level efficiency and cost attribution unmeasured.

MCP adds communication steps and context-management operations such as tool schema discovery and injection that can substantially affect end-to-end latency and token usage even when final answer quality is unchanged.

MCP workflows include hidden protocol work before a user query is processed, such as the host fetching tool schemas from servers and injecting them into the LLM prompt, which makes schema-related tokens hard to separate from user-provided content.
Agent execution frequently involves multi-turn internal loops (planning, tool selection, retries) that are invisible to end users but expensive in both tokens and time.

ProMCP decomposes a tool-augmented MCP interaction into a six-stage pipeline: S1 user-to-LLM prompting, S2 LLM-to-client planning, S3 client-to-server tool call, S4 server-to-client tool response, S5 client-to-LLM context update, and S6 LLM-to-user answer synthesis.
Per-stage latency can be aggregated into three user-meaningful segments: tool-plan latency (S1-S2), tool-execution latency (S3-S4), and answer-synthesis latency (S5-S6).

Attribution should distinguish LLM usage tokens (provider-reported or locally tokenized prompt/response pairs) from protocol token footprint (the tokenized size of MCP artifacts such as schemas, JSON tool calls, and tool results measured under the same tokenizer) to separate protocol representation cost from model reasoning cost.

Session initialization (the initialize handshake, the tools/list schema-discovery request, and readiness confirmation) should be treated as a first-class part of the MCP lifecycle and logged for token footprint and latency, because it can incur substantial cost before any user prompt is issued.
During MCP session initialization, the tools-discovery step dominates initialization cost because the server must serialize and transmit verbose JSON schemas for every available tool.

HTTP/SSE connections show significantly lower session-initialization latency than STDIO, attributed to STDIO's cold-start penalty of spawning a new subprocess per connection while HTTP servers remain warm and persistent.
condition: at session initialization

statement: Once a connection is established, tools-discovery latency is negligible across both STDIO and HTTP/SSE, confirming that schema transmission is bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound.
condition: after the connection is established

statement: Latency should be measured at stage boundaries with monotonic clocks inside the instrumented component: LLM calls (S1, S2, S6) from request dispatch to completion or last streamed chunk, and tool calls (S3, S4) from JSON-RPC request emission to response receipt, so per-stage delays are comparable across STDIO and networked deployments.

MCP efficiency cost depends on both protocol-mandated artifacts (schema discovery, JSON-RPC serialization) and client/host orchestration choices (prompt construction, context retention, streaming behavior).

MCP deployment topology can be characterized along two axes: where the LLM runs (local vs cloud) and whether the client is customizable or off-the-shelf, yielding the L-Cust, C-Cust, and C-OTS configurations.

For off-the-shelf clients, protocol-level traces are not directly exposed, so the six-stage pipeline must be reconstructed post-hoc from exported conversation logs (for example conversations.json) by mapping tool-use messages to stages and deriving per-stage latency from timestamp deltas.
condition: off-the-shelf client topology (C-OTS)

statement: For every event in the pipeline, a structured log record should capture identifiers (run_id, task_id, stage, phase label, direction), high-resolution send/receive timestamps and derived stage latency, model/tool/transport metadata, token accounting (input, output, total plus injected-payload footprint), and truncated payload previews.

On the simpler MCP-Bench task set with customized clients, the planning phase accounts for over half of total tokens (52-63%), reflecting the fixed overhead of loading comprehensive tool schemas for the model to reason about.
condition: MCP-Bench tasks with customized clients (L-Cust, C-Cust)

statement: When tool calls fail to return usable results, clients fall back on the LLM's internal knowledge to produce an answer, shifting part of the workload to the final-answer phase.
condition: when tool calls fail to return usable results

statement: In the off-the-shelf client configuration the planning token share drops to about 2.1% because the client uses deferred (lazy) loading to avoid injecting the full tool list.
condition: off-the-shelf client topology (C-OTS)

statement: The measurements span 20 MCP servers and 169 tools across MCP-Bench (15 servers, 151 tools, 30 single-server tasks) and MCP-Universe (8 servers, 125 multi-step tasks).

On the more complex MCP-Universe task set with a customized cloud client, the dominant token cost moves to the tool-result phase (77.5%), driven by the heavy retrieval requirements of open-ended queries.
condition: complex open-ended tasks (MCP-Universe) with a customized cloud client (C-Cust)

statement: Local model behavior diverges sharply on complex tasks: Mistral 3.2 mirrors the high-volume retrieval pattern (81.8% tool-result tokens) while LLaMA 3.2 stays compact (20.0% tool-result tokens), so model choice reshapes the token profile.
condition: complex open-ended tasks (MCP-Universe) with local models

statement: The off-the-shelf client configuration exhibits extreme token amplification, exceeding 1.2 million total tokens (orders of magnitude higher than custom setups) on complex agentic workflows, because unconstrained tool interactions inflate costs exponentially.
condition: off-the-shelf client (C-OTS) on complex open-ended tasks

statement: The dominant contributor to off-the-shelf-client tool-result token usage is the WebSearch tool, because it retains full multi-document search outputs across turns, causing re-consumption of retrieved content during subsequent reasoning and answer synthesis.
condition: off-the-shelf client (C-OTS) using a WebSearch tool

statement: The off-the-shelf client injects the entire raw JSON tool response, including metadata, headers, and auxiliary fields, directly into the context for maximum information fidelity, whereas custom clients wrap results to extract only task-relevant data.
Tool-result verbosity is a client orchestration-policy choice, not an MCP protocol requirement, and wrapping tool results to task-relevant fields substantially reduces token cost.
On simple MCP-Bench tasks, local execution has a massive speed advantage, with Mistral 3.2 reaching near-instantaneous total latency (~1.28s) and a planning phase under one second.
condition: simple tasks (MCP-Bench) with a local model

statement: The local small-model latency advantage is fragile: on complex MCP-Universe tasks Mistral 3.2 total latency jumps to ~73.5s driven by a spike in the planning phase (~46.8s) with extreme variance (standard deviation ~113s).
condition: complex open-ended tasks (MCP-Universe) with a small local model

statement: Small local models are highly efficient for simple tool use but struggle to process the heavier context windows of open-ended tasks, often hanging or processing inefficiently during the planning stage.
condition: open-ended tasks with heavy context windows

statement: LLaMA 3.2 exhibits latency scaling with low variance (3.90s to 41.43s across datasets, standard deviation ~18.2s), indicating stable and predictable model behavior under increasing task complexity.

The customized cloud-API configuration has an inherent latency floor of roughly 22s even on simple tasks, dominated by the planning phase (~14.6s), so its primary bottleneck is pre-filling and processing of system prompts and tool definitions rather than tool execution.
condition: customized cloud-API client (C-Cust)

statement: For custom cloud setups, planning cost nearly doubles as task complexity rises (from ~14.6s to ~25.3s), confirming that prompt processing remains the dominant latency contributor.
condition: customized cloud-API client (C-Cust)

statement: The off-the-shelf client shows consistently high total latency (~95s) driven almost entirely by the final-answer phase (~81s, over 86% of execution time), and this output bottleneck scales to ~382s on the complex MCP-Universe task set.
condition: off-the-shelf client topology (C-OTS)

statement: The bottleneck location shifts with client implementation: custom environments (L-Cust, C-Cust) suffer an input bottleneck determined by how quickly the model parses tool definitions and plans, while off-the-shelf environments (C-OTS) suffer an output bottleneck where unconstrained generation and streaming dominate.
The verbose, streaming response style of the desktop off-the-shelf client incurs a severe penalty on user-perceived latency, correlating with its massive token volume.
condition: off-the-shelf client topology (C-OTS)

statement: Despite substantial overhead differences across topologies, all configurations maintain high task success and answer quality (85-100% accuracy and 4.06-4.91 human-assessed quality on a 1-5 scale).
Optimization that targets orchestration overhead does not require quality trade-offs on these benchmarks, since overhead and answer quality vary independently.
condition: on the benchmarks evaluated

statement: Profiling commercial off-the-shelf clients via post-hoc reconstruction from exported logs (conversations.json) rather than real-time introspection captures aggregate latency but cannot measure precise millisecond-level jitter or internal retries that produce no user-visible message.
condition: off-the-shelf client topology (C-OTS)

statement: Measurements taken on a single hardware configuration may not transfer directly, since OS-level scheduling or STDIO buffer-size differences on Linux or macOS could introduce minor performance deviations in the local topology.

Because the six-stage decomposition isolates tool execution (S3-S4) from prompting, planning, and synthesis (S1-S2, S5-S6), the framework directly reveals the regime shift and quantifies orchestration overhead relative to tool latency even when tools are heavy.
When profiling stage latency, streaming should be disabled so that chunked-response buffering does not blur stage boundaries, isolating protocol-hop latency from token-streaming jitter.
condition: when millisecond-level stage-wise latency attribution is required

statement: To keep cost attribution stable across profiling runs, use a bounded agent horizon (maximum 10 rounds), bounded retries (maximum 3), and sequential rather than parallel tool execution.
Caching should be disabled for tool execution during profiling to avoid artificially reduced latency measurements.
condition: during latency profiling

statement: An off-the-shelf client operates as a black box with provider-managed streaming and buffering enabled, so token delivery is fragmented and may introduce latency unrelated to protocol communication.
condition: off-the-shelf client topology (C-OTS)

statement: Absolute token counts are not directly comparable across models such as Mistral 3.2, LLaMA 3.2, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 because of differences in subword segmentation schemes and vocabulary construction.

Token counts across the compared model tokenizers show near-perfect linear correlation (Pearson r >= 0.99), so the cross-tokenizer inexactness is a constant factor rather than interpretation blur, and relative performance rankings and latency trends remain invariant regardless of the underlying tokenizer.
Static tool provisioning — exposing every available tool to the LLM on each query — does not scale: it inflates token cost, degrades tool-selection accuracy, and collides with context-window limits.
A single tool schema typically costs about 200-800 tokens, so a 100-tool catalog consumes roughly 20,000-80,000 tokens before any user query or response.
LLM accuracy degrades as context length grows, so injecting irrelevant tool definitions adds noise that lowers tool-selection accuracy.
Manual, human-curated tool subsets cut token count but are inflexible and fail to capture the semantic nuance of user intent.

There is a real gap: no semantic, query-aware tool-selection mechanism exists for standardized tool protocols like MCP, and prior RAG work targets document retrieval rather than executable-tool selection.
The proposed approach indexes each MCP tool as a dense embedding and, per query, retrieves only the top-K most relevant tools (typically 3-5) instead of exposing the full 50-100+ catalog.

Build each tool's embedding document from a structured template — tool name, purpose, expanded capabilities, and parameter descriptions — to give the matcher multiple semantic anchors for user intent.
The query path embeds the user query, runs a top-K similarity search over the tool vector store, then optionally applies a similarity-threshold filter and an optional hybrid-search rerank.
condition: threshold filtering and reranking are optional stages

statement: An optional feedback loop can log which tools were actually invoked, task success or failure, and user feedback, and use that signal to refine embeddings or tune retrieval parameters.
A working reference stack for semantic tool discovery: Milvus vector store, text-embedding-ada-002 (1536-dim) embeddings, the official Python MCP SDK, and GPT-4o as the downstream LLM.
Evaluate a tool-selection system with Precision@K, Recall@K, F1@K, Hit Rate@K and MRR, and quantify savings with a Token Reduction Rate measured against the all-tools baseline.
On a benchmark of 140 queries over 121 tools from 5 MCP servers, semantic retrieval cut tool-related tokens by 99.6% while achieving a 97.1% hit rate and 0.91 MRR at K=3.
Precision falls monotonically as K rises (92.1% at K=1 down to 26.5% at K=10) while recall climbs (31.5% up to 90.6%), so F1 peaks at K=3 (58.4%).
K=3 is the optimal operating point for most deployments — it gives the best F1 (58.4%), a 97.1% hit rate, 0.91 MRR, and 99.6% token reduction.
condition: for most deployments on the tested setup
exception: the optimal K may not transfer to embedding models or LLMs other than the tested text-embedding-ada-002 and GPT-4o

statement: Raising K above 3 buys only marginal hit-rate gains (about 1.5 percentage points from K=3 to K=10) while sharply cutting precision.
Counterintuitively, giving the LLM fewer but more semantically relevant tools improves its tool-calling accuracy rather than harming it (92.1% precision at K=1).

The accuracy gain from fewer tools is attributed to reduced decision complexity: with a small relevant set the model spends more reasoning on parameter construction and execution than on tool disambiguation.
The greater-than-99% token reduction is domain-invariant — it holds across all five servers and every K value tested.
Retrieval latency stays under 91ms across all K values and servers — negligible next to LLM inference — so K can be chosen on accuracy grounds alone rather than latency.

Servers whose tools have distinct domain vocabulary (GitHub, MySQL) reach near-perfect hit rate at low K, whereas servers with overlapping tool descriptions (Filesystem) need a higher K for adequate recall.
condition: depends on how semantically distinct the server's tool descriptions are

statement: Small tool catalogs benefit disproportionately in F1 because a larger fraction of the catalog is relevant to any query, so retrieval metrics must be read relative to catalog size.
condition: when the tool catalog is small

statement: Ambiguous queries (for example 'help me with my project') lack the semantic specificity to pin a domain and cause the retriever to return a mixed, cross-domain tool set.
To handle ambiguous queries, fold conversational context (prior tool use, active server sessions) into the query embedding, or prompt the user to clarify before retrieving.
Semantically overlapping tools (read_file, write_file, copy_file, move_file) make the retriever surface related-but-wrong tools, shown by Filesystem's low MRR (0.84-0.89).
To disambiguate semantically similar tools, add parameter-level matching or tool-usage-frequency signals to break ties among the near-duplicate candidates.

Cross-domain queries that need tools from several servers (for example 'commit the DB schema changes to GitHub') often fail to surface tools from all domains within top-K under single-query retrieval.
For cross-domain queries, decompose the user intent into sub-tasks and retrieve tools for each sub-task (multi-query retrieval) rather than issuing a single retrieval.

For graceful degradation, when no tool clears the similarity threshold, fall back to returning the top-K tools anyway so the LLM always receives a minimal tool context; alternatives are falling back to the all-tools baseline for low-confidence queries or routing to a human operator.
condition: when the threshold filter would otherwise return an empty set

statement: New tools must be embedded and indexed before they become discoverable (about 2 seconds per tool); catalogs that change often warrant a scheduled re-indexing pipeline that also refreshes embeddings when tool descriptions change.
For high-throughput deployments, caching the retrieved tool set for common recurring query patterns can cut latency further.
condition: high-throughput deployments with recurring query patterns

statement: Retrieval quality is fundamentally bounded by how informative tool descriptions are: poorly documented tools are under-retrieved regardless of embedding model, while well-differentiated descriptions with distinct domain vocabulary retrieve best.

The same semantic-retrieval mechanism extends to multi-agent routing (embed agent capability descriptions for two-level agent-then-tool retrieval), cross-organizational federated discovery (per-org vector indexes merged by a coordination layer, preserving ownership and access control), and dynamic tool composition (mine the feedback loop for co-occurring tool chains and retrieve whole pipelines).
Effectiveness at enterprise scale (thousands of tools) is not yet validated — the study covers only 121 tools, 5 servers, and 140 queries.
Results rely on a single embedding model (text-embedding-ada-002) and GPT-4o, so the optimal K=3 and the accuracy findings may not transfer to other embedding models or LLMs.
exception: other embedding models or downstream LLMs may require different parameters

statement: The evaluation is single-turn and offline, so multi-turn conversational context and online A/B behaviour are unmeasured and could shift the results.

The economic stakes are large: at about $0.03 per 1K input tokens, 50,000 tokens of tool definitions cost roughly $1.50 per request, or about $1.5M per month at 1M requests — the waste that semantic filtering removes.
Semantic tool discovery makes large-scale, multi-server MCP deployments economically feasible and technically performant, removing a key barrier to adopting tool-augmented LLMs in production.
Keep the retrieval architecture modular — independently replaceable embedding models, vector stores, and retrieval parameters — so it can adapt as the MCP ecosystem and embedding technology evolve.
As available tools grow from hundreds to thousands, intelligent tool discovery shifts from a nice-to-have optimization to a necessity.
condition: as tool counts scale into the thousands

statement: The implementation, the benchmark dataset (140 queries with ground-truth tool selections across 5 MCP servers), and the evaluation framework are released open-source for further research.
MCP host clients must re-serialize and re-inject the full tool-catalog schemas on every conversational turn because the underlying chat-completions APIs are stateless.

The recurring per-turn overhead of full MCP schema injection (the 'Tools Tax') is roughly 15,000-55,000 tokens in typical four-to-six-server deployments and can exceed 150k under aggressive tool sprawl.
condition: in typical four-to-six-server MCP deployments; practitioner-reported ranges

statement: The per-session Tools Tax scales with turns and catalog size as K times the sum of per-tool definition tokens, approximated by K*(alpha*N + a description term), with a community heuristic of alpha in [200,500] tokens per tool.
For a representative enterprise setup of N=120 tools, K=30 turns and alpha=395, the Tools Tax reaches about 1.42M tokens consumed before the user's first message.

The Tools Tax precipitates three cascading failures: economic (order-of-magnitude higher per-session spend), cognitive (reasoning collapse as context fills), and adversarial (an enlarged tool-poisoning attack surface).
One published benchmark reports CLI-equivalent workflows at $3.20 versus MCP at $55.20 for the same 10,000 operations.
condition: practitioner-reported benchmark

statement: Once effective context utilization crosses roughly 70% (the useful-context ratio rho falls below about 0.3), LLM reasoning quality collapses: models hallucinate tool arguments, confuse similar tools, and lose multi-step coherence.
condition: when context utilization exceeds ~70%

statement: Every injected schema token proportionally inflates the transformer key-value cache, adding GPU memory pressure, fragmenting allocations, and increasing time-to-first-token.
Disciplined FinOps audits repeatedly attribute 40-60% of total agent API spend to schema tokens.
condition: practitioner-reported FinOps audits

statement: A Tool Poisoning Attack lets an adversary who controls a single tool description inject instructions that hijack the agent without the tool ever being invoked, and the attack surface grows with the number of in-context schemas.

Published per-server MCP footprints range from about 1,200-3,000 tokens per turn for small servers up to about 55,000 for the full GitHub suite (93 tools) and about 54,600 for a 106-tool enterprise database catalog.
condition: practitioner audit figures treated as minima, assuming perfect description hygiene and counting only tool definitions

statement: Tool Attention is a drop-in middleware-layer mechanism that generalizes self-attention over tokens to gated attention over tools, replacing eager uniform schema injection with dynamic, query-conditioned tool selection.

Tool Attention decomposes into three components: an Intent-Schema Overlap (ISO) score from sentence embeddings, a state-aware gating function enforcing preconditions and access scopes, and a two-phase lazy schema loader.
The Intent-Schema Overlap score is the cosine similarity between the sentence embedding of the current user query and the embedding of a tool's compact summary.
For each tool, precompute offline a compact summary (its name plus a shortened natural-language description, target <=60 tokens) together with its sentence embedding.

The gating function admits a tool only when its ISO score meets the threshold theta and the agent's current state satisfies the tool's preconditions; the turn's active tool set is the top-k of gated tools ranked by ISO.
condition: a tool is admitted only if ISO>=theta and state satisfies its preconditions

statement: A tool whose expected Total Attention Energy for a query is negligible can be excluded from the prompt without changing the agent's decision, and the ISO score serves as a cheap embedding-space proxy for that expected attention energy.
condition: when the tool's expected attention energy for the query is negligible

statement: Gating is dual-purpose: it cuts injected schema tokens for efficiency and shrinks the tool-poisoning surface for security, because a poisoned description that does not cosine-match the user's intent is gated out and never reaches the model's attention layers.
Two-phase lazy loading keeps all N compact tool summaries resident in context (about 40 tokens each, Phase 1) and promotes the full JSON schema only for the gated top-k tools on demand (Phase 2).
The two-phase layout preserves tool discoverability because summaries stay visible, while eliminating the cost of carrying unused full schemas, and the stable Phase-1 pool is prompt-cacheable.

A hallucination-rejection gate deterministically rejects any tool call the model emits for a tool not in the turn's active set, returning a structured error, so routing false negatives are caught downstream; this is what makes aggressive gating safe.
condition: when the model calls a tool whose full schema was not promoted this turn

statement: The router's per-turn cost is O(N log N), dominated by top-k extraction over N cosine scores (sub-millisecond for N<=10,000 with a FAISS flat inner-product index), while the query-encoder forward pass runs in about 30-60 ms on CPU.

Default to the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 encoder (22M parameters, 384-dimensional) for its accuracy/latency trade-off; higher-capacity encoders raise recall only about 2-4 points while roughly tripling embedding latency, which is not worthwhile because the hallucination gate already absorbs false negatives.

Calibrate the ISO threshold theta once per deployment on a held-out set of 100-200 (query, ground-truth-tool) pairs by sweeping theta in [0.10,0.50] in 0.02 steps and choosing the value that maximizes F1 (typically about 0.22-0.32).
condition: per deployment, using a held-out query/tool calibration set

statement: Set top-k conservatively large (about 8-12) and rely on the threshold for precision, hedging against encoder drift and ambiguous queries.
Self-documenting tool names substantially outperform cryptic ones on retrieval F1 (for example, a descriptive search_customer_orders_by_date_status_and_amount beats a generic query_db).

Write tool summaries in the voice of a user's intent rather than the implementer's; an LLM-based summary-regeneration utility cut average summary length by 63% while improving retrieval F1 by 8 points.

Specify preconditions as small Python predicates over authoritative agent state (such as is_authenticated, has_prior_tool_output, or milestone_reached); unlike semantic routing they give deterministic filtering that an adversarial paraphrase cannot bypass.

In the experiments the hallucination gate triggered on 2.3% of turns; the model recovered on the next turn in 78% of those cases and correctly asked for clarification in the remaining 22%, with no observed unrecoverable failure.
condition: in the 120-tool synthetic simulation

statement: Because the Phase-1 summary pool is stable across turns it earns full prompt-cache credit, and placing per-turn Phase-2 schemas immediately before the user message yielded an 84% cache-hit rate over a 30-turn session versus 22% for naive full-schema injection.
condition: measured in the simulated 30-turn session

statement: Emit a structured observability event for every routing decision (turn id, candidate scores, state-gated-out set, active set, Phase-1 and Phase-2 token counts, and latency) to feed FinOps dashboards and audit for gate misfires.
The paper's evaluation is a simulation harness that constructs the exact tokenized prompts and counts their tokens, not a live end-to-end agent evaluation.

In the evaluation only per-turn token counts and effective context utilization rho are directly measured (with tiktoken, cl100k_base); task-success rate, P50/P95 latency, marginal cost, and LLM-judge reasoning quality are projections, not live measurements.

statement: The synthetic testbed comprises 120 tools across six servers (GitHub 30, Filesystem 10, Database 20, Slack 15, Web 10, Jira 35) averaging about 394 tokens per schema, for an aggregate full-schema injection cost of about 47,300 tokens per turn.

The five compared configurations are B1 Full-Schema (all 120 schemas every turn), B2 Static Pruning (a manual 30-tool subset), B3 Simple Retrieval (cosine top-k=10 full schemas, no gating or lazy loading), B4 CLI Lazy Discovery (CLI list/help, no schemas in context), and Tool Attention (theta=0.28, k=10, MiniLM-L6, two-phase, hallucination gate).

The six evaluation metrics are tokens per turn and effective context utilization rho (both directly measured) and task-success rate, P50/P95 latency, marginal cost per task, and LLM-judge reasoning quality (all projected).
