statement: The paper's central thesis is that protocol-level efficiency (context engineering), not raw context length, is the binding constraint on scalable agentic systems.
The MCP/Tools Tax is a protocol-design artifact born of treating every catalog tool as always-on context, rather than an inevitable cost of agentic AI.

In the reference implementation the router over-fetches a candidate slate of max(4k, 20) tools from the vector store, then filters them by threshold and precondition and stops at the first k survivors.
The reference lazy loader caches full schemas in an LRU keyed by tool id (default capacity 256), fetching from a registry or disk only on a cache miss.
The reference implementation normalizes embeddings so that a FAISS inner-product index computes cosine similarity directly.

Decouple intelligence (deciding what to do) from execution (carrying it out) in tool-calling LLM agent architectures so the agent reasons once and the plan is executed many times without further reasoning.

In prevailing agent architectures the agent must reason about every tool invocation in every session, consuming tokens proportional to the number of actions even when the task was already solved before.
Agent-in-the-loop token cost grows quadratically (O(N^2)) because each of N steps reprocesses the accumulated intermediate results in its context window.
Recurring multi-step tool tasks separate cleanly into a one-time, intelligence-intensive design phase and a repeated, mechanical execution phase that requires no intelligence.

Implement the orchestration layer as an MCP Mediator: a single component that is simultaneously an MCP server exposing workflow tools upward to agents and an MCP client connecting downward to downstream MCP servers.

The Mediator pattern leaves downstream MCP servers unmodified and unaware of the engine (transparency), and makes any MCP-compliant tool server automatically available to workflows via auto-discovery (composability).

Under the Mediator the agent interacts only with workflow-level abstractions (create_workflow, run_workflow) while the engine handles connection management, routing, retries, and data flow (separation of concerns).

Design (Phase 1) has two token-intensive sub-phases that happen once: exploration (enumerate downstream tools via tools/list and make trial invocations to learn response schemas) and blueprint construction (reason about resource types, relationships, and ordering).
During exploration, discover downstream tools by calling tools/list to enumerate tools and their JSON-Schema parameter specs, and make trial invocations to observe real response structures.
In execution (Phase 2) the stored blueprint is triggered by a single run_workflow call and the engine autonomously executes all steps with zero agent involvement.
The reusable artifact is a workflow blueprint: a JSON document specifying an id, description, parameterized inputs, an error-handling strategy, and an ordered sequence of steps.

Design blueprints to be declarative (describe what, not how), parameterized (inject runtime values via {{params.*}} templates), portable (versionable in Git, shareable, cron-schedulable), and inspectable (human- and machine-readable for validation and audit).
Constrain the workflow DSL to five step types (call, loop, parallel, pipe, collect), which cover most multi-tool orchestration while keeping the semantics formal and the failure modes predictable.
The call step invokes a named MCP tool on a downstream server with template-resolved parameters and is the atomic unit of execution.
The loop step iterates over a resolved array, executing a sub-step for each item with per-item context injected (for example, iterating over namespaces).
The parallel step runs independent branches concurrently via Promise.allSettled to maximize throughput.
condition: branches are independent operations

statement: The pipe step chains steps sequentially, each receiving the previous step's output, enabling data-transformation pipelines.
The collect step aggregates a sub-workflow's outputs into a single batch so an agent can review the batch rather than individual items (a hybrid agent-engine pattern).

Deliberately exclude conditionals, variables, and string manipulation from the DSL: branching requires agent reasoning, data flows implicitly via steps.<id> (eliminating scoping bugs), and data shaping remains the agent's responsibility.
Constraining a JSON-based DSL is intentional because such DSLs tend to evolve into accidental programming languages, and a firm boundary avoids that fate.
Resolve {{expression}} templates with JMESPath for structured data extraction and a dot-path fallback for simple property access.
When the entire value is a single template expression, return the raw resolved value (preserving arrays and objects) instead of stringifying it, to enable type-safe data flow between steps.
condition: the entire value is a single template expression

statement: Maintain a resolver context that stores each completed step's output at steps.<stepId>, making it available to all later steps via templates and giving implicit data flow without explicit variable declarations.

Treat every downstream tool as a pure function (name, params) -> result, routed via a toolName->serverClient table built by calling tools/list on each server at initialization, connecting over stdio, SSE, or streamable-HTTP transports.

Offer three error strategies: abort (stop on first failure, for critical pipelines), continue (log and proceed, for best-effort sync), and retry (retry up to n times with backoff, for transient failures).
With collectErrors enabled, accumulate all errors alongside successful results to enable partial-success workflows, which are essential for large-scale infrastructure operations.
condition: collectErrors is true

statement: Perform two-tier validation at design time: structural errors (missing IDs, unknown step types) block saving, while tool warnings (tools not found in connected servers) are non-blocking.
The workflow engine's per-execution cost is roughly 150 tokens (one trigger plus one tool call), i.e. O(1) regardless of blueprint complexity.
Break-even between the two architectures occurs at about K*=0.04 executions, meaning the engine recovers its one-time design cost after roughly 4% of a single full agent execution.
condition: cost amortized over K repeated executions

statement: On a 67-step CMDB synchronization (2 MCP servers, 38 namespaces, 13 nodes, 22 resource types) the engine cut per-execution token cost by over 99% and built a graph of 1,200+ nodes and 2,800+ relationships in about 42 seconds with zero errors and zero agent tokens.
The engine delivered a 40-80x latency improvement over agent-in-the-loop execution by eliminating the 1-5 seconds of inference latency per agent reasoning cycle.
exception: latency is still bounded by downstream API response times

statement: Workflow-engine execution is deterministic and idempotent (the same blueprint against the same cluster state produces the same tool calls), unlike agent-in-the-loop execution, which is probabilistic and may hallucinate tool names, build invalid queries, or exceed the context window mid-task.

Achieve idempotent writes by using Cypher MERGE operations exclusively, so re-running a workflow updates timestamps and adds resources without creating duplicates, which is essential for scheduled synchronization.
condition: writing to a graph database on a scheduled or repeated basis

statement: Under the workflow engine token cost does not scale with cluster size, whereas under the agent baseline it grows super-linearly due to context accumulation.

Ablation shows template resolution is essential (every step fails without it), parallel execution reduces execution time by about 38% for independent fetches, and the continue error strategy is critical for production reliability.

Prefer a declarative workflow blueprint over generated code for the roughly 80% case of deterministic, repetitive orchestration because it gives sandboxing (only MCP tools are invocable), inspectability (parseable JSON), design-time validation against live schemas, and reliable LLM editability.
condition: the task is deterministic, repetitive orchestration (about the 80% case)
exception: for complex conditional logic, generated code or continued agent reasoning is more appropriate

statement: The dual-role MCP Mediator pattern generalizes beyond workflow engines to aggregation, caching, audit, and rate-limiting, in each case without requiring modification of downstream MCP servers.

Use the collect step for hybrid agent-engine workflows: the engine executes the mechanical parts (for example fetching crash-looping pod logs in a loop) and returns a single batch for agent reasoning, giving O(1) reasoning passes instead of O(N).
condition: not all steps in the task can be fully automated

statement: The design-once, trigger-many pattern generalizes to any domain with repeated multi-step tool orchestration (for example incident response, security auditing, data lineage, compliance reporting), each projected to save more than 90-95% after a one-time design.
condition: the domain involves repeated multi-step tool orchestrations

statement: The reported token figures are estimated from per-step cost assumptions rather than measured with a specific model's tokenizer, because the system is model-agnostic.
Tasks that require runtime branching still require agent involvement because the workflow DSL does not support conditionals.
condition: the task requires runtime conditional branching

statement: The reference implementation is single-process; distributed execution across multiple engine instances remains future work.

The reference implementation is compact: roughly 1,250 lines of TypeScript across 12 source files running as a single Node.js process, with minimal dependencies (the MCP SDK, jmespath, zod, and uuid).
The engine exposes six workflow-management tools to agents: create_workflow, run_workflow, list_workflows, get_workflow, validate_workflow, and delete_workflow.

The reported savings are a conservative lower bound because the per-step estimates omit cumulative context growth and real agent reasoning adds planning, self-correction, and backtracking that increase consumption.
Amortized token savings exceed 99% once the task is repeated about five or more times, with steady-state marginal savings of roughly 99.989%.
condition: cost is amortized over five or more repeated executions

statement: Stated future work includes distributed multi-engine execution, conditional step types with bounded complexity, and empirical benchmarking across diverse LLM providers.

Deploy MCP-enabled agentic workflows on serverless FaaS platforms rather than monolithic VMs to gain modularity, autoscaling, and pay-per-request cost efficiency, but design explicitly around FaaS statelessness.

Hosting agentic workflows on VMs is resource-intensive and lacks elasticity, and tends to under- or over-provision resources because of high request variability and non-deterministic agent execution flows.
FaaS platforms are inherently stateless, which precludes natively persisting agent and workflow memory inside the platform.

Decompose an agentic pattern such as ReAct into separate composable agent functions (Planner, Actor, Evaluator), each deployed as its own FaaS function and orchestrated as a FaaS workflow (e.g. AWS Step Functions) with explicit message passing.

Modeling an agentic workflow as a single monolithic function risks exceeding the FaaS per-function execution timeout (15 minutes on AWS Lambda); decomposing it into independent functions avoids that timeout.
condition: on FaaS platforms that impose a per-function execution timeout

statement: Decomposing agent roles into separate functions lets each role be configured independently (its own system prompt, memory, and resource allocation).

Because agent functions are stateless, different workflow iterations and different workflow executions can be served by shared or distinct function instances, maximizing FaaS resource efficiency and lowering cost and cold-start time versus per-application deployment.

A ReAct FaaS workflow is cyclic: the Evaluator either returns a successful result to the user or routes control back to the Planner for a revised plan, iterating until success or a user-defined maximum iteration count.
LangGraph models each workflow step as a node (an LLM call, data processing, or MCP tool call); nodes share a common read/write state and are connected into a graph following the action sequence.
LangGraph's in-memory graph state is transient — it lives only for the duration of a function's execution — so it must be passed downstream as explicit messages between the composed functions.

Give the Actor agent a conditional edge so its Tool-call node runs only when the LLM requests one or more tools, feeding tool output back to the LLM until the plan completes or LangGraph's default loop limit (25 supersteps) is reached.

In classic stateless FaaS, each user request in a multi-turn session starts from a clean slate because transient agent/workflow memory is lost when the workflow completes, causing the workflow to fail on follow-on requests.

Persist agent memory in an external store (FAME uses DynamoDB) keyed by a session_id with a per-request invocation_id, so multi-turn workflows can recall prior context; the Evaluator writes memory once per invocation and FAME injects retrieved memory into the Planner's node.

Carrying prior request/response pairs forward as cumulative Client Memory gives session continuity but can cause previously completed agent tasks to be repeated, incurring redundant token cost and latency.

Injecting full agent memory (user request, LLM interactions, per-agent tool I/O, and final response) lets the Planner avoid repeating unsuccessful strategies and lets the Actor skip redundant tool calls.
When appending to the external memory store, write only the new memory state produced by the current invocation, since prior invocations' memory is already persisted, to avoid duplicate writes.
Decoupling memory from the Lambda functions and storing it externally preserves the stateless FaaS execution model while still enabling stateful multi-turn agentic workflows.
External memory persistence is modular enough to allow pre-processing before storage — e.g. summarization or knowledge-graph distillation — to reduce context-size explosion.
Externally persisted agent memory doubles as an inherent provenance and audit record for traceability.

Even with a large LLM context window, injecting stale or off-topic memory can distract the model and raises latency and cost, so retaining only the right state in memory is an important design decision.
LLMs are stateless, so any prior conversational state needed in the context window must be supplied by the agent or framework.

MCP servers cannot be embedded directly inside FaaS functions because they use console (stdio) or network transports; wrap each MCP server as a FaaS function exposed over HTTP (e.g. an AWS Lambda Function URL) to mimic a remote MCP server while gaining FaaS scaling and billing.
MCP defines a JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol at the data layer; its transport layer uses stdio for local servers and HTTP POST with Server-Sent Events for remote servers.
Remote MCP servers reduce developer setup overhead, can serve complex tools, and can be shared across agents, whereas local (colocated) servers make the workflow self-contained.

Generate the FaaS wrapper for an MCP server automatically — parse the server source into an AST to detect imports, constants, and decorator-tagged tool functions, then inject the handler, telemetry, and caching code — instead of hand-writing per-server glue.

FAME's generated wrapper uses the aws.mcp-lambda-handler package to route MCP HTTP requests to the server logic, adds a lambda_handler entry point, supports both synchronous and asynchronous tool functions, and packages a Docker image pushed to ECR with IAM permissions, memory, and timeout configured.
FaaS functions are billed per invocation by their configured memory and execution time, so both peak memory and latency directly drive cost.
FaaS functions incur cold-start overheads and have container retention periods that both affect latency and cost.

Provision MCP servers intelligently across independent, workflow-unified, or global-unified deployment strategies to manage cost, since colocating MCP servers with their workflows in the same data center reduces latency and eases manageability.
The stateless nature of FaaS also prevents persistence of local file artifacts across invocations, which must be addressed by externalizing those artifacts.
Encapsulating each MCP server as an isolated function enhances security, because tool calls can invoke external libraries and perform complex operations.

FAME achieved up to 13x latency reduction, 88% fewer input tokens, and 66% cost savings with improved workflow completion rates, evaluated on two applications (research-paper summarization and log analytics) using the ReAct pattern.
condition: for the two evaluated applications under the tested memory and caching configurations

statement: Per-agent system prompts that describe each agent's role provide grounding that lowers hallucinations (goal deviations), and augmenting the agent with external knowledge via MCP services can further mitigate reasoning errors.
The ReAct pattern interleaves reasoning, action, and observation steps and improves upon plain Chain-of-Thought prompting for complex, tool-using tasks.

Cache an MCP tool's output and reuse it for repeat requests with identical arguments, but only when the tool is deterministic for those arguments (e.g. downloading a persistent URL or a pure computation).
condition: the tool's output is deterministic for the given input arguments

statement: MCP tool-output caching is especially valuable when a user session issues multiple request sequences that require the same pre-processing (e.g. downloading a file before repeatedly analyzing it).

Attach a developer-configured time-to-live (TTL) to each cached MCP result to bound staleness and cache bloat — a short or zero TTL for volatile data (e.g. stock prices) and a long or infinite TTL for immutable fetches (e.g. a DOI download).

Implement the MCP cache by hashing the tool's name plus parameters into a cache key, storing the output in S3 under that key with the TTL in S3 object metadata, and on each call returning the cached object if the key exists and its TTL is unexpired, otherwise executing the tool and caching the result.
MCP tools that return large content inline (e.g. full file contents) can quickly overwhelm the agent's memory and LLM context window.

Have MCP servers store large tool outputs in S3 and return the S3 URL instead of the inline content, and download S3-referenced inputs only when actually needed, so large blobs never enter the LLM context window.

MCP servers can be deployed singleton (each server its own Lambda function with its own memory) or consolidated (all of an application's servers fused into one Lambda exposing all tools, with memory set to the peak of the constituents).

Singleton MCP deployment can be cheaper due to lower per-function memory footprint but incurs more cold-start delays because each server is managed independently, whereas consolidating servers reduces cold-start latency at a higher per-invocation cost.

Agents do not reliably use memory that is injected into their context — even when prior user requests, tool inputs/outputs, and inter-agent messages are available, the LLM sometimes ignores them and repeats the same tool calls, raising latency and cost.

Add an explicit system-prompt instruction telling the agent to check previous tool responses in the conversation history and reuse that data before issuing new tool calls (only calling again if the data is unavailable or the parameters differ); this markedly reduces redundant work and MCP tool calls.

Configurations that combine MCP caching and agent memory (C, M, M+C) consistently outperform the empty-memory (E) and naive client-memory (N) baselines on end-to-end latency across both evaluated applications.
condition: for the two evaluated applications and workloads

statement: With no persisted memory, follow-on queries in a session fail (DNF) because the workflow has no reference to the artifact fetched in the first query, leading the LLM to hallucinate.
The configuration combining agentic memory and MCP caching (M+C) consistently outperformed all other configurations, achieving up to a 13x end-to-end speedup.

The latency gain from caching/memory comes mainly from reduced Actor-agent execution time, because the Actor passes an S3 URL for a cached document downstream instead of ingesting the full document into its context.

Output-token counts stay roughly constant across configurations because they are constrained by the task's output format, whereas input-token counts vary widely and directly drive both latency and monetary cost.
Empty and naive-memory configs re-ingest the entire document text for every agent action, causing excessive input-token usage; enabling caching and agent memory dropped input tokens by roughly 85%.
Enabling agent memory and MCP caching reduced input tokens by up to 88%.

LLM token costs dominate total spend (roughly 61-94%), while FaaS agent-execution cost is around 13% and MCP Lambda cost around 3%, so optimizing token consumption yields far larger savings than optimizing FaaS execution.

LLM cost is directly proportional to input plus output tokens and dwarfs FaaS execution cost — on the tested workload the token charge for 50K input tokens was about an order of magnitude (~9x) more expensive than ~50s of the three-function ReAct Step Function execution.
condition: on the tested GPT-4o-mini workload

statement: Agent-memory and MCP-cache optimizations reduced total monetary cost by up to about 66%.

MCP cache benefits appear only after a warmup: the first query pays an S3 upload cost (~0.19s) with no cache benefit, while subsequent queries hit the cache and cut MCP latency (e.g. ~33% on a repeated document fetch).
condition: on repeated calls after the cache has been warmed

statement: MCP caching reduces token consumption because a cache hit returns only the S3 handle rather than the full content (e.g. an ~83% input-token drop on a repeated document query).
MCP caching alone yielded roughly a 28% improvement in MCP execution time and a ~51% reduction in tokens.

Singleton MCP deployment has higher cold-start overhead than consolidated deployment, because each client invocation targets a different MCP Lambda that each pays its own cold start, whereas a consolidated server is initialized once and reused across subsequent tool calls.
The consolidated MCP deployment showed fewer cold starts, faster stabilization, and stable latency and per-call cost that were equal to or better than the singleton deployment.
When consolidating multiple MCP servers into one function, set the function's memory to the maximum required by any constituent server.
LLM non-determinism can cause sporadic workflow failures (DNF) even for queries that succeeded on prior identical runs, for example by passing incomplete parameters to a downstream MCP server.

No failures (DNFs) were observed for the caching and agent-memory configurations (C, M, M+C), indicating that caching plus agent memory makes the workflow more reliable by giving the agent information to rely on instead of re-executing everything from scratch.
Persisting memory and caching mechanisms can mitigate the impact of an LLM's inherent randomness (temperature) in practical agentic workflows.

LangGraph differs from Graph-of-Thoughts and AutoGen by modeling the workflow as an explicit graph over a shared persisted state rather than prescribing a reasoning strategy, giving developers greater control over execution flow such as branching, conditional routing, and retries.

Prompt the Planner agent to take the user query plus the available tool descriptions and emit a plan that specifies which tools to use and the sequence of tool calls, returned as strict JSON with a tools_to_use list and a reasoning field.
Prompt the Actor agent to execute the specified tools in the exact sequence given by the Planner's plan to address the user query.

Prompt the Evaluator agent to take the plan, the result, and the current/maximum iteration count and respond with strict JSON containing success, needs_retry, reason, and feedback fields, setting success=true only when the result answers the user query.
Constrain each ReAct agent's LLM to return only valid JSON in a fixed schema, so that downstream agents and the workflow's branching logic can parse each agent's output deterministically.

Bound the ReAct iteration loop with an explicit maximum: the Evaluator may set needs_retry=true only while iteration_count is below max_iterations and must set it false once the maximum is reached, guaranteeing termination.
Require the Evaluator to include a feedback field (only when needs_retry=true) that the Planner then consumes to design a revised plan that avoids the prior attempt's failure.
Design an MCP server as a capability-oriented agent interface that exposes capabilities, not as a one-tool-per-endpoint mirror of the underlying API.

Wrapping one MCP tool per API endpoint does not scale for large platforms: it forces the LLM to act as a routing layer (work a server-side switch does better) and spends context on tool definitions that could be spent on reasoning.
An MCP client loads every tool definition (name, description, parameter schema, and annotations) into the LLM context window when it connects, consuming context before the developer types any prompt.
Reducing an MCP server's exposed tools sharply cuts context overhead: Harness went from 130+ tools costing roughly 26% of a 200K-token context on tool definitions to 11 tools at about 1.6%.

Use a registry-based dispatch model: expose a small set of generic verb tools and keep a declarative registry that maps each resource type to its API operations, so adding a new module means adding one declarative resource definition rather than new tool schemas and the LLM's tool vocabulary stays constant as the platform grows.
A registry-based MCP design can cover 125+ resource types across 30 toolsets while exposing only 11 generic tools.

Research on long-context LLM behavior (Liu et al., 'Lost in the Middle') indicates models struggle to use information placed deep in a long context, and irrelevant 'dead' context dilutes the attention weight carried by the relevant context.

Keep the tool-definition share of the context window within a conservative budget (stay well under ~40% total utilization), because when several MCP servers are loaded together their tool definitions stack and can consume a large fraction of context before any prompt.
condition: when multiple MCP servers are loaded in the same client

statement: Anthropic's engineering team reported that switching from direct tool calls to code-based tool invocation reduced a 150,000-token workflow to about 2,000 tokens, roughly a 98.7% reduction.
The MCPAgentBench benchmark found that nearly all evaluated models lose more than 10 points in task efficiency as tool-selection complexity increases, still completing tasks but wasting tokens.
Lunar.dev reported that five MCP servers of thirty tools each inject 150 tool definitions at 200-500 tokens apiece, adding roughly 30,000-60,000 tokens of pure tool-metadata overhead.

IDE and model tool caps constrain how many tools an agent can load at once (Cursor about 80, OpenAI 128, Claude about 120), so a lean tool surface is needed to run several MCP servers together without exceeding the cap.

Scalekit's 75-run benchmark on identical GitHub tasks found CLI 10-32x cheaper and 100% reliable versus MCP's 72%, with a simple query costing 1,365 tokens via CLI against 44,026 via MCP, almost all of the MCP cost coming from injecting 43 tool schemas the agent never used.
The CLI-versus-MCP cost gap is caused by tool-schema bloat and naive tool design, not by the MCP protocol itself; a well-designed MCP server removes the cost argument against MCP.
Prefer CLI over MCP when the agent already knows the tool from training data (e.g. gh, kubectl, terraform): it pays zero schema overhead and produces terse, predictable output.
condition: the agent has strong training-data knowledge of the tool

statement: Prefer CLI over MCP for composition-heavy work where a single piped command chains several operations, avoiding the N LLM round-trips an equivalent MCP flow would require.
condition: operations compose naturally via piping/chaining

statement: Scalekit found that adding an approximately 800-token skills document to CLI usage cut tool calls and latency by about a third.

Prefer MCP over CLI for runtime capability discovery: when a platform's API surface is larger than what the agent knows from training, a describe/discovery tool lets the agent learn capabilities at runtime instead of guessing undocumented API calls.
condition: the platform's API surface exceeds the agent's training knowledge

statement: Prefer MCP over CLI for authorization in multi-tenant, multi-user environments: CLI hands the agent ambient credentials (your token), whereas MCP can enforce per-user OAuth, explicit tool boundaries, and structured audit trails.
condition: multi-tenant or multi-user environment

statement: Prefer MCP over CLI when safety matters: a CLI agent can run arbitrary shell commands, whereas an MCP server constrains the agent to declared tools with typed inputs and protocol-level guardrails.

Ship a companion skills layer that turns raw MCP tool access into guided, IDE-native, multi-step workflows, so the agent does not have to infer domain concepts, correct ordering, and API calls from scratch.

A skills layer can be structured in three levels: an auto-loaded shared agent-instruction file per IDE, server-side prompt templates any MCP client can invoke, and individual SKILL.md files acting as slash commands.

The shared agent-instruction file should teach the agent the tool set, the platform's scoping hierarchy (account -> org -> project), dependency ordering (verify referenced resources exist before creating dependents), and how to extract context from platform URLs.
Encode multi-step workflows as prompt templates with explicit phase gates ('do not proceed until this step is done') so the agent follows ordered checkpoints instead of improvising the ordering.

A skills layer reduces exploratory round-trips (agents otherwise need 3-5 discovery calls to learn a resource model), makes the agent follow correct dependency ordering on the first attempt, and cuts token waste from failed calls and retries.

Define each agent command or skill once in a canonical location and symlink it into each IDE's command directory ('define once, deploy to every IDE') to keep a single source of truth across Claude Code, Cursor, and Windsurf.
Require explicit human-in-the-loop confirmation for all write operations (e.g. via MCP elicitation): the agent states what it intends to do and the user approves or rejects before execution.
Make destructive operations fail closed: block delete entirely when the MCP client cannot support a confirmation/elicitation flow, so there are no silent deletions.
condition: client does not support elicitation
exception: delete is blocked entirely rather than executed

statement: Provide a read-only mode that lets agents observe but not act, for shared environments, demos, or observe-only use.
condition: shared environments, demos, or observe-only use

statement: Expose secret resources as metadata only (name, type, scope) and never return the secret value itself.

Add operational guardrails for resource-mutating agents: configurable rate limits (e.g. default 10 requests/second), automatic retries with backoff for transient failures, and bounded pagination to prevent runaway list operations.

Support both a stdio transport for zero-configuration local IDE integration and a session-based streamable-HTTP transport for remote/team deployment, with sessions reaped on a timeout, CORS restricted, and per-IP rate limits.

Let every tool accept an optional URL parameter and auto-extract scope identifiers (account, org, project, resource) from a pasted platform URL, so the agent gains context without the developer specifying it manually.

Allow startup-time toolset filtering (an environment variable listing enabled toolsets) so the agent only sees resource types from the modules a team actually uses and is not distracted by irrelevant tools.
condition: a team uses only specific modules of the platform

statement: Registry-based dispatch collapses round-trips: a single call to a diagnose verb can return a complete execution analysis (structure, timing, logs, root cause) that a CLI agent would otherwise assemble from 4-5 chained API calls.
Tools make LLMs productive, but exposing the tool definitions to the LLM is context-expensive, creating a tension between usefulness and token cost.
Exposing more than a handful of tools (loading hundreds of API operations) quickly hits the context-window limit or incurs prohibitive token cost.
condition: when many tools are exposed statically

statement: A refined Dynamic Toolset for MCP achieved up to 160x token reduction versus a static toolset while maintaining a 100% task success rate across diverse tasks.
Dynamic Toolsets reduce token usage by an average of 96% for input tokens and 90% for total token consumption.
The token savings make it practical to build MCP servers exposing hundreds of tools without overwhelming the LLM's context window.
Embeddings-based semantic search effectively helps an LLM find the right tools within a large toolset.
Pure semantic search fails when the LLM has no visibility into what tools exist: it may not even attempt a search.
condition: when available tool categories are not surfaced to the LLM

statement: A vague prompt such as 'how many deals do we have?' confuses the LLM because it cannot know that 'deal' maps to a HubSpot deal without visible tool context.
Including an outline of tool categories in the tool description (progressive search) improves discoverability and makes the LLM more likely to attempt a tool search.
Category-based discoverability depends on the quality of the input Gram Functions or OpenAPI documents, whereas semantic search does not carry that dependency.
condition: quality of the source API/function documentation

statement: Move tool-schema retrieval into a separate describe_tools function so the LLM loads input schemas only for the tools it actually intends to use.
Input schemas are a large share of total tokens, often 60-80% of token usage in static toolsets.
Expose three core tools - search_tools (semantic search plus a tool-category overview), describe_tools (on-demand schemas), and execute_tool - to combine discoverability with token efficiency.
Let search_tools accept tag filters such as source:hubspot or hubspot/deals so the LLM can narrow the search precisely.
Tool descriptions supply structure and discoverability while semantic search supplies efficiency and natural-language discovery; combining both scales without sacrificing usability.
A static toolset's token usage grows roughly linearly with toolset size, whereas a Dynamic Toolset keeps token consumption roughly constant from 40 to 400 tools.

In benchmarks, input tokens fell about 96.7% on simple tasks and 91.2% on complex tasks; total tokens fell about 96.4% and 90.7% respectively, even after accounting for extra output tokens from more tool calls.
The benchmark held a 100% success rate - the LLM called the expected underlying tools with the expected arguments - across all toolset sizes and task complexities.
condition: tested with Claude Sonnet 4.5; success defined as calling the expected tools with expected arguments

statement: Dynamic Toolsets require about 2-3x more tool calls than a static toolset because the LLM must search for and then describe tools before executing them.
The extra tool calls raise execution time by roughly 50% on average compared with a static toolset.
condition: average across the benchmarked tasks

statement: For longer-running agents the execution-time overhead is expected to shrink, possibly below the static toolset, because already-discovered tools are reused without new search or describe calls.
condition: longer-running agents, after tools are already discovered

statement: Despite roughly 2x more tool calls, total tokens and runtime do not increase, because input tokens are cut by more than 96%.
A complex multi-tool workflow typically runs 6-8 total tool calls (versus 3 for a static toolset): about 2-4 search_tools, one describe_tools, and three execute_tool calls.
condition: complex multi-tool workflow
exception: an 8-call pattern occurs when a search does not return the expected results, which is common with larger toolsets

statement: Batch schema requests: call describe_tools once for all the tools you intend to use rather than once per tool.
Tool-call count can be reduced by combining search_tools and describe_tools into a single call, at the cost of higher token usage.
condition: when minimizing tool-call count matters more than token cost

statement: Conversation history acts as a cache for already-loaded tool descriptions and schemas, cutting redundant token usage in multi-step workflows.
Adding new tools to a Dynamic Toolset does not increase baseline token usage, so the approach scales naturally as an API grows.
Specialized 'code mode' environments can sidestep context limits entirely, but they demand significant engineering investment and domain expertise that most teams lack.
exception: most teams lack the engineering investment and domain expertise required

statement: In client-mode conformance testing the framework starts a test server for the chosen scenario, spawns the client under test against it, captures the MCP protocol interactions, and runs conformance checks against the captured traffic.
In client mode the framework appends the test server URL as the final command-line argument to the client command and sets the MCP_CONFORMANCE_SCENARIO environment variable to the scenario name.
Scenario-specific data such as OAuth client credentials is passed to the client under test as a JSON object in the MCP_CONFORMANCE_CONTEXT environment variable.
condition: the scenario requires additional context

statement: Server-mode testing requires the server under test to already be running before the conformance tool is invoked; the framework connects to it as an MCP client, and the SDK owns the server lifecycle (start, health-check, cleanup).

A client under test must derive its protocol lifecycle from the protocol version it is asked to run: dated versions through 2025-11-25 use the stateful lifecycle (initialize handshake) while the 2026 draft (2026-07-28) uses the stateless lifecycle (per-request _meta).
condition: the protocol version the client is asked to run

statement: When --spec-version is passed, its resolved value is forwarded to the client process as MCP_CONFORMANCE_PROTOCOL_VERSION, which example clients may use directly as their protocolVersion.
exception: the SDK hard-codes its protocol version and ignores the forwarded value

statement: An explicitly requested --spec-version that falls outside a scenario's applicability window skips that scenario with exit 0.
exception: --force is passed, which runs the scenario anyway

statement: An SDK that does not yet pass all conformance tests can record a baseline of known failures so CI passes on those known failures while still catching regressions.

With an expected-failures baseline, a scenario that fails and is not in the baseline exits 1 (unexpected regression) and a scenario that passes while still listed in the baseline also exits 1 (stale baseline whose entry must be removed).

The conformance repo ships a composite GitHub Action so SDK repos do not have to write their own conformance scripts, taking inputs such as mode, url or command, suite, scenario, and expected-failures.
In server-mode CI the SDK must start its own server and health-check it as ready (for example, polling the /mcp endpoint until it responds) before invoking the conformance action.

The sdk subcommand clones an SDK repository at a given ref, builds it, and runs the local conformance build against it, serving as the inner-loop tool for scenario authors and the basis for cross-SDK CI.
The sdk subcommand requires --mode client or --mode server, and each invocation tests exactly one side, so client and server pass or fail independently.

Build and run commands for each official SDK are looked up by name from a built-in KNOWN_SDKS table with no config file required in the SDK repo, and resolution order is CLI flag over built-in entry so any field can be overridden per invocation.

The tier-check subcommand evaluates an MCP SDK repository against SEP-1730 (the SDK Tiering System) and can run quickly with --skip-conformance or against a running conformance server via --conformance-server-url.
A new scenario is added by creating src/scenarios/<name>/, implementing the Scenario interface with start(), stop(), and getChecks(), and registering it in src/scenarios/index.ts.
The coverage metric that matters for the conformance repo is spec coverage — how much of the protocol the scenarios exercise — rather than harness polish.
The repo uses npm (not pnpm or yarn), and pnpm-lock.yaml and yarn.lock must not be committed.
Contributors should open an issue to discuss a bug or a proposed scenario before opening a PR.

Do not point an agent at the repo to find bugs generically; give it a concrete target such as a specific spec MUST/SHOULD with no scenario yet or an open issue, because generic bug-hunting on a test harness yields low-signal PRs.

Prefer one scenario with many checks over many scenarios with one check each — the strongest scenario-design rule in the repo — because each scenario often spins up its own HTTP server whose per-scenario overhead multiplies across every SDK's CI, it is less code to maintain, and progress reads as pass N/M checks (finer-grained signal).
Apply the granularity heuristic 'would it make sense for someone to implement a server/client that does just this scenario?', and if two scenarios would always be implemented together, merge them.
Keep scenarios separate only when they are genuinely independent features or mutually exclusive, such as a server that deliberately does not implement certain stateful features.
condition: the scenarios are genuinely independent or mutually exclusive

statement: When a PR adds scenarios, start with one end-to-end happy-path scenario carrying many checks, and do not add a 'step 1 only' plus a 'step 1+2' scenario because the larger one subsumes the smaller.
A conformance check must use the same id for its success and failure outcomes, flipping status and errorMessage rather than branching into separate foo-success and foo-failure slugs.
Optimize check code for Ctrl+F on the slug: repetitive check blocks are acceptable because finding the failing check by its slug beats unwinding a clever shared helper.
Reuse ConformanceCheck and other shared types from src/types.ts instead of defining parallel shapes.

Do not reimplement the runner: a new subcommand that selects scenarios, runs them, prints a summary, and computes an exit code must go through the existing client/server commands (subprocess via process.execPath) or shared helpers rather than a parallel suite-map or summary loop.
Every conformance check should include specReferences pointing to the relevant spec section.

Check severity follows the spec keyword — MUST/MUST NOT map to FAILURE and SHOULD/SHOULD NOT map to WARNING — and because CI treats WARNING as a failure, a Tier-1 SDK must still satisfy SHOULD-level requirements.

A check whose prerequisite is missing (the server lacks a diagnostic fixture tool, rejects the probe, or advertises a feature it does not serve) must be reported as failed via notTestable()/untestableCheck() with the missing prerequisite named and details.untestable set true, not as SKIPPED.

SKIPPED reads as green in every consumer (pass counts, exit codes, expected-failures), so it is reserved for checks that are legitimately not applicable, such as an optional capability the server never declared, spec-version inapplicability, or a documented harness gap.
Scenario descriptions must state precisely what is required versus optional and must not accidentally promote a MAY or SHOULD to a MUST in the prose.
When unsure about spec details such as OAuth parameters, audiences, or grant types, consult the actual modelcontextprotocol spec rather than guessing.

Verify a SEP scenario's requirement levels against the SEP's spec diff (the change under docs/specification/draft/), not the SEP markdown summary or the conformance PR description, because the governing keyword is the one in the spec text.

traceability.json is a generated per-SEP map of which declared check IDs are actually emitted when the suite runs against the reference SDK, and because it derives from a real run, dynamic template-literal check IDs resolve to their concrete values.
In the traceability manifest 'tested' means a scenario emitted the check ID, not that any SDK passes it; per-SDK pass/fail results live in tier-check instead.
A SEP absent from the traceability manifest has no conformance artifacts and must be treated as not-started by consumers.

A new scenario should ship with both a passing example (usually by extending the everything-client or everything-server rather than a new file) and a negative test — a deliberately-broken implementation plus a case asserting the check emits FAILURE or WARNING — because a passing run only proves the check does not false-positive, not that it catches anything.

Before opening a PR, npm run build and npm test must pass, non-trivial scenario changes should be run against at least one real SDK (typescript-sdk or python-sdk), and shared-infrastructure changes to the runner or tier-check should also be run against go-sdk or csharp-sdk.

In client-mode execution the runner starts the test server(s) on available ports, spawns the client process with the server URL as the final argument, the test server captures the MCP interactions, the runner captures client stdout/stderr, scenario checks run, and results are written to results/<scenario>-<timestamp>/ (server mode writes results/server-<scenario>-<timestamp>/).

All CLI arguments are validated with Zod schemas before reaching the runner: client mode requires a non-empty command, an existing scenario, and a positive-integer timeout, while server mode requires a valid HTTP/HTTPS URL and existing scenarios and defaults to all scenarios when none is specified.
Each conformance result is a ConformanceCheck object written to checks.json carrying id, name, description, status, timestamp, specReferences, and details fields.

The conformance suite imports the canonical protocol TypeScript types from vendored spec-types/<version> copies rather than from @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, so it can test draft spec versions before any SDK has implemented them.
The vendored spec-types files must not be hand-edited; they are refreshed with npm run sync-schema -- <sha-or-ref>, and the SOURCE file records the spec commit the current copies came from.

A scenario imports the schema version matching its source.introducedIn, and a Connection implementation imports the schema version whose lifecycle it implements (stateful maps to 2025-11-25, stateless to draft).

The reference conformance server implements every feature required for conformance testing — the full tool, resource, and prompt set, logging at all levels, completion for prompt and resource arguments, list-changed notifications, and resource subscription/update notifications — so one suite can verify conformance across all SDK implementations.

Example conformance servers must use the standardized naming conventions — test_ prefixes for tools and prompts and the test:// scheme for resources, with names describing the feature under test — so a single test suite verifies conformance across every SDK implementation.

An SDK's example conformance server must reproduce the reference server's automatic behaviors — dynamically registering a tool, resource, and prompt about two seconds after startup and updating a watched resource about every three seconds — so the suite can exercise MCP notifications without manual triggers.

A conformance server should serve MCP over Streamable HTTP and must catch and handle promise rejections from notifications when no client is connected so that unhandled notification errors do not crash it.

The no-dns-rebinding-protection example server intentionally omits DNS rebinding protection as a negative test expected to FAIL the dns-rebinding-protection scenario, and this pattern must not be used in production: real localhost servers must use createMcpExpressApp() or the localhostHostValidation() middleware.

In the authorization-server-migration scenario (SEP-2352), when the server's Protected Resource Metadata flips to a new authorization server and a new issuer surfaces on a 401, the client MUST re-register with the new authorization server rather than reuse the previous server's client credentials.
condition: the Protected Resource Metadata changes the authorization server / a new issuer appears on a 401

statement: In the resource-mismatch scenario, per RFC 8707 and the MCP spec, a client MUST validate that the resource field in Protected Resource Metadata matches the server URL it is accessing and MUST abort authorization on a mismatch rather than proceed.

In the offline-access scenario (SEP-2207), when Authorization Server metadata lists offline_access in scopes_supported, a client SHOULD include refresh_token in its grant_types client metadata and MAY include offline_access in the authorization request scope, while the server's PRM deliberately does not list offline_access.
condition: the Authorization Server metadata lists offline_access in scopes_supported

statement: In the pre-registration scenario, when the server does not support Dynamic Client Registration, the client MUST use the pre-registered credentials supplied via context (Basic authentication) rather than attempt DCR.
condition: the server does not support Dynamic Client Registration

statement: In the scope-handling scenario, a client SHOULD follow the scope parameter from the initial WWW-Authenticate header in a 401 response when selecting the authorization scope.

In the issuer-parameter scenario, when a server advertises authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported true and returns an iss value in the authorization redirect, a conformant client validates the iss value before proceeding.
condition: the server advertises authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported and returns an iss value

statement: In the elicitation-defaults client scenario (SEP-1034), a client MUST apply default values for omitted fields in an elicitation response — across string, integer, number, enum, and boolean schemas — before sending the response to the server.

In the http-standard-headers scenario (SEP-2243), on Streamable HTTP POST requests a client MUST send an Mcp-Method header mirroring the JSON-RPC method and an Mcp-Name header mirroring params.name or params.uri for tools/call, resources/read, and prompts/get requests.

In the http-custom-headers scenario (SEP-2243), a client that supports the x-mcp-header extension MUST mirror each annotated tool-parameter value into an Mcp-Param-{Name} header, encoding plain-ASCII values directly and Base64-encoding non-ASCII, whitespace-affected, or control-character values.

In the http-custom-headers scenario (SEP-2243), a client MUST NOT add Mcp-Param headers for parameters lacking an x-mcp-header annotation, MUST omit the header when the parameter value is null or absent, and MUST reject tool definitions whose x-mcp-header is empty, on a non-primitive type, duplicated (including case-insensitively), or contains a space, colon, non-ASCII, or control character.

In the json-schema-ref-deref scenario (SEP-2106), although SEP-2106 permits the full JSON Schema 2020-12 vocabulary including $ref, an implementation MUST NOT automatically dereference a $ref that resolves to a network URI, because a network $ref is an SSRF and fetch-DoS vector.
exception: the $ref is a same-document JSON Pointer such as #/$defs/Foo or an internal $anchor, which may be resolved

statement: In the mrtr-client scenario (SEP-2322), a client in the Multi-Round Tool Resolution flow MUST echo requestState back unchanged on retry, MUST NOT include requestState when the server sent none, MUST use a different JSON-RPC id on the retry, MUST treat a result without a resultType as complete, and MUST NOT carry inputResponses or requestState into any other request.

In the request-metadata scenario, a client MUST send the MCP-Protocol-Version header on every POST, populate _meta on every request with all three required fields, keep the MCP-Protocol-Version header matching _meta.protocolVersion, and retry with a supported version when its first choice is rejected.

When latching per-request-id check results, a single non-conformant request is a violation even if later requests are conformant, so the harness ranks severity and never lets a later better status overwrite a worse one.

In the sse-retry scenario (SEP-1699), a client MUST respect the SSE retry field by waiting the specified milliseconds before reconnecting, MUST treat a graceful stream closure as reconnectable and reconnect via GET, and SHOULD send the Last-Event-ID header on reconnection for resumability.

In the caching scenario (SEP-2549), a server MUST include ttlMs and cacheScope hints on cacheable results (tools/list, prompts/list, resources/list, resources/templates/list, and resources/read), with every ttlMs a non-negative integer and every cacheScope either public or private.

In the dns-rebinding scenario, a localhost MCP server MUST validate the Host or Origin header to prevent DNS rebinding attacks, rejecting non-localhost Host/Origin values and accepting valid localhost ones (see GHSA-w48q-cv73-mx4w).

In the elicitation-defaults server scenario (SEP-1034), a server that requests elicitation MUST include default values in the elicitation schema across string, integer, number, enum, and boolean field types.

In the elicitation-enums scenario (SEP-1330), a server encodes elicitation enum schemas by shape: an untitled single-select uses an enum array, a titled single-select uses oneOf with const/title, the legacy titled form uses the deprecated enumNames, an untitled multi-select uses an array with items.enum, and a titled multi-select uses an array with items.anyOf.

In the http-standard-headers server scenario (SEP-2243), a server MUST reject a request whose Mcp-Method or Mcp-Name header disagrees with the JSON-RPC body — or is missing when the body carries a name — returning HTTP 400 with the JSON-RPC error -32020 (HeaderMismatch).

In the http-standard-headers server scenario (SEP-2243), a server MUST treat MCP request-header names case-insensitively but header values case-sensitively, MUST accept leading and trailing whitespace in the Mcp-Name value per RFC 9110 section 5.5 (excluding optional whitespace before evaluating), and MUST reject a request where a custom header is omitted while its value is present in the body.

In the input-required-result scenario (SEP-2322), a server responds with InputRequiredResult (carrying inputRequests and/or requestState) and the client retries with inputResponses and echoed requestState; the server MUST include the resultType field, MUST NOT return InputRequiredResult on unsupported methods, MUST reject tampered requestState with an error, MUST include inputRequests only for declared client capabilities, and returns a JSON-RPC error for protocol-level input errors.

In the json-schema-2020-12 scenario (SEP-1613, SEP-2106), a server MUST preserve JSON Schema 2020-12 keywords in tool definitions through tools/list — not stripping $schema, $defs, or additionalProperties (SEP-1613) and keeping composition (allOf/anyOf), conditional (if/then/else), and reference ($anchor) keywords intact (SEP-2106).
In the lifecycle server scenario, a server MUST respond to an initialize request with a valid structure, and any server-provided session ID MUST use only visible ASCII characters.

In the resources server scenario, for a non-existent resource a server SHOULD return -32602 (Invalid Params) rather than an empty contents array, and SHOULD include the requested URI in the error data field.

In the sse-multiple-streams scenario (SEP-1699), a server supports multiple concurrent SSE streams by giving each POST request its own stream with a unique stream ID, while the standalone GET stream (without Last-Event-ID) is limited to one per session.

In the sse-polling scenario (SEP-1699), a server SHOULD send a priming event carrying an id and empty data on POST SSE streams and SHOULD send a retry field to control client reconnection timing, and it must be able to close an SSE stream mid-operation and resume, replaying events when the client reconnects with Last-Event-ID including via GET.

In the stateless scenario (SEP-2575), every error response MUST carry the request's JSON-RPC id, and a server MUST reject a request whose _meta is missing — or whose _meta omits io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion, clientInfo, or clientCapabilities — with -32602 (Invalid params).
In the tools server scenario, a tool name MUST be 1 to 64 characters and match the pattern ^[A-Za-z0-9_./-]+$.

In the tasks capability scenario (SEP-2663), a server MUST advertise the io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension, gate the v2 task surface on capability negotiation, and support SEP-2575 per-request capability overrides.

In the tasks dispatch scenario (SEP-2663), the removed v1 methods tasks/result and tasks/list MUST reject with -32601, server-directed task creation works without a client task hint (the legacy v1 task param is tolerated and ignored on sync tools), a fast operation MAY skip task creation and return a sync ToolResult, every non-task response carries the SEP-2322 resultType 'complete' discriminator, and with strong consistency tasks/get immediately after a CreateTaskResult MUST resolve while tasks/get with an unknown taskId MUST return -32602.

In the tasks composition scenario (SEP-2663 with SEP-2322), when a tool gathers input via the MRTR loop on tools/call and then escalates to async on the final round returning a CreateTaskResult, the inlined result of the eventual task MUST reflect the answer gathered during the MRTR phase, so an implementation that wires MRTR and tasks as independent surfaces fails the end-to-end check.

In the tasks required-capability scenario (SEP-2575 with SEP-2663), if a tool declares task support as 'required' and the client did not declare io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks at initialize, the server MUST reject the call with the MissingRequiredClientCapability error code -32021, and the error data SHOULD carry a requiredCapabilities object mirroring InitializeRequest capabilities so the client can self-describe what to add.
condition: the tool's declared task support is 'required' and the client did not declare the tasks extension at initialize

statement: In the tasks request-state scenario (SEP-2663), because SEP-2663 defines no requestState field on the tasks-v2 wire, a CreateTaskResult MUST NOT carry requestState and a DetailedTask (tasks/get response) MUST NOT carry requestState regardless of status; SEP-2322's InputRequiredResult.requestState is unrelated to the tasks wire.

In the tasks wire-fields scenario (SEP-2663), the tasks-v2 wire uses the renamed fields ttlMs and pollIntervalMs, enforces a no-early-TTL-expiry rule, and omits the v1 related-task _meta key on tasks/get's inlined result because the taskId already appears at the root.

The tasks status-notifications scenario is a documented harness gap left SKIPPED: SEP-2663 delivers notifications/tasks over the SEP-2575 subscriptions/listen stream, but the harness observes SSE frames on the tools/call POST response and so misses notifications from spec-following servers.
A conformant MCP authorization server's metadata response MUST include client_id_metadata_document_supported set to true to signal Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD) support.

A check whose prerequisite is missing — the server under test lacks a diagnostic fixture, rejects the probe, or advertises a feature it does not serve — MUST NOT report SKIPPED, because SKIPPED is excluded from pass/fail counts, exit codes, and the expected-failures baseline and so hides the gap; it MUST instead fail with an errorMessage naming the missing prerequisite and may sit in an expected-failures baseline until the prerequisite exists, while SKIPPED stays correct only for a genuinely inapplicable check such as an optional capability the server never declared or spec-version inapplicability handled by the runner.

The MCP SDK tier audit evaluates 48 non-experimental features — 36 core, 6 transport, and 6 protocol — plus 5 experimental Tasks features (tasks/get, tasks/result, tasks/cancel, tasks/list, and tasks status notifications) that are informational only and do not count.

Under SEP-1730, Tier 1 (Fully Supported) requires a 100% conformance pass rate, Tier 2 (Commitment to Full Support) requires at least 80%, and Tier 3 (Experimental) has no minimum, where the pass rate is passed/(passed+failed)*100 from the conformance suite.

SEP-1730 requires Tier-1 support for new protocol features before each new spec version's release (timeline agreed per release by complexity) versus within 6 months for Tier 2, issue triage within 2 business days versus within 30 calendar days, and P0 critical-bug resolution within 7 calendar days versus 14.

Under SEP-1730 an issue is triaged when it receives its first label (triage is labeling and validity assessment, not resolution), and a P0 critical bug is a security vulnerability with CVSS at or above 7.0 or a core-functionality failure blocking connection establishment, message exchange, or use of core primitives.

SEP-1730 Tier 1 requires a stable release at or above 1.0.0 with no pre-release suffix and a documented breaking-change (clear-versioning) policy, comprehensive documentation with examples for all non-experimental features, a published dependency-update policy, and a published roadmap with concrete steps; Tier 2 requires at least one stable release, basic docs covering core features, a published dependency policy, and a published plan toward Tier 1.

Only date-versioned scenarios (for example 2025-06-18 and 2025-11-25) count toward tier scoring while draft and extension scenarios are listed separately as informational, and the --spec-version flag filters date versions cumulatively (2025-06-18 includes 2025-03-26 plus 2025-06-18) but returns exact matches for draft and extension.

SEP-1730 relegation rules drop an SDK from Tier 1 to Tier 2 if any conformance test fails continuously for 4 weeks, and from Tier 2 to Tier 3 if more than 20% of conformance tests fail continuously for 4 weeks.
To enable automated tier reporting, an SDK repository must apply a consistent 12-label issue taxonomy of 3 type, 5 status, and 4 priority labels.
exception: the repository uses GitHub's native issue types, which satisfies the type-label requirement without separate type labels

statement: A tier audit must pre-flight before doing anything else by verifying GitHub CLI authentication (gh auth status) and that the conformance server is reachable, stopping immediately and telling the user if either check fails, because the everything server must already be running for server conformance to be measured.

The tier-check --branch flag should always be included, derived from the local checkout's current branch when not explicitly given, so that policy signal-file checks run against the correct branch rather than the repository's default branch.

The deterministic tier-check CLI computes all deterministic checks — server and client conformance pass rate (with per-spec-version breakdown), issue triage, P0 resolution, label taxonomy, stable release, policy signal files, and spec tracking — and emits JSON, while the AI evaluations cover only documentation coverage and policy substance.
When no client conformance command is provided, client conformance tests are skipped and noted as a gap, but a skipped client suite alone must not block tier advancement.
condition: no client conformance command is detected or provided

statement: An expected-failures baseline must be read and cross-referenced when interpreting raw conformance pass rates, because a low pass rate caused entirely by unimplemented OAuth scenarios (a scope gap) is very different from one caused by broken core functionality.
The documentation and policy evaluations judge substance using only the files the deterministic CLI already found, and must not search for policy files in other locations.

Tier 1 requires ALL of: server and client conformance pass rate at 100% (date-versioned scenarios only), issue-triage compliance at or above 90% within 2 business days, all P0 bugs resolved within 7 days, a stable release at or above 1.0.0 with no pre-release suffix, a documented breaking-change policy, all non-experimental features documented with examples, a published dependency-update policy, and a published roadmap with concrete steps tracking spec components.

Tier 2 requires ALL of: server and client conformance pass rate at or above 80% (date-versioned scenarios only), issue-triage compliance at or above 80% within 1 month, P0 bugs resolved within 2 weeks, at least one stable release at or above 1.0.0, basic docs covering core features, a published dependency-update policy, and a published plan toward Tier 1; if any Tier 2 requirement is unmet the SDK is Tier 3.

Conformance results should be presented as a single matrix combining server and client results, where the client category is derived from the scenario name (an auth/ prefix means Auth and everything else means Core) and all server scenarios are Core.

In the conformance matrix, failures clustered in Client: Auth at the newest spec version indicate new auth features not yet implemented — a scope gap rather than a quality problem — whereas failures in Server or Client: Core are more concerning.

When the P0 count is high (more than 2) but other Tier-2 metrics such as conformance, triage compliance, and docs are strong, this likely indicates P0 labels are being misused for enhancements or lower-priority work, so the audit should recommend a P0 label audit rather than treat the high count as an automatic hard blocker.
condition: the P0 count exceeds 2 while other Tier-2 metrics are strong

statement: A sep-NNNN.yaml traceability file (per SEP-2484) maps each normative sentence from a SEP's spec diff to a check: ID when testable or an excluded: reason when not, the CLI generates the skeleton and the author fills the rows from the spec diff, and by convention the SEP number is the PR number in modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol.

When extracting requirements from a spec diff, quote the whole normative sentence rather than just the matched line, because a MUST or SHOULD keyword in a lead-in sentence is inherited by its bullets and regex matching alone is insufficient (issue #243) — the surrounding context of pronouns, 'the server', and 'such cases' must be read.

RFC 2119 severity maps to YAML as follows: MUST, MUST NOT, SHALL, SHALL NOT, and REQUIRED produce a check: row at FAILURE severity, SHOULD and SHOULD NOT produce a check: row at WARNING severity, and MAY and OPTIONAL produce no row at all and are skipped entirely.

A requirement becomes an excluded: row only when a MUST or SHOULD cannot be protocol-observed by the harness, and no exclusion may be written on the author's own authority: every exclusion needs user sign-off, with clearly-excluded rows batched into one question and borderline rows (internal-state, UI or human-facing, or precondition phrasing) asked one per row.

Traceability YAML conventions: a check uses the same id for SUCCESS and FAILURE, slugs are lowercase-kebab derived from the verb phrase, a check: row leads with the check: key (then text, then optional url) while an excluded: row leads with text: (then excluded, then optional issue), and all check: rows precede all excluded: rows, grouped and separated by one blank line and never interleaved.
When a requirement is ambiguous or you are not confident, leave it as a TODO: row rather than guessing, because humans review the traceability yaml before scenarios are written.
A traceability row's effective spec reference is row.url falling back to file.spec_url, so a requirement sourced from a different spec page than the file's spec_url must carry a full url: override.

Before recommending a brand-new scenario file, look for an existing scenario the new checks can fold into (the repo prefers fewer scenarios with more checks): derive the suite directory from the requirement subject (clients to client/, servers to server/, authorization servers to authorization-server/), search it for scenarios on the same spec area, and recommend a host by path or state explicitly that none fits.

When reviewing a conformance scenario PR, treat the SEP's actual spec diff as ground truth and read the RFC-2119 sentences yourself rather than trusting the PR description or SEP summary, and if the SEP includes a conformance-test-case table that table is authoritative for the cases it lists, so a table/prose mismatch is a spec gap to flag rather than silently resolve.

Review the traceability YAML by diffing its rows against the spec sentences you extracted and flagging any row that paraphrases rather than quotes, claims a keyword level the spec does not support, or asserts something the spec never says.

A scenario check has adequate spec backing only if a fully spec-compliant implementation would not fail it; if a compliant implementation would fail, or two compliant SDKs in different languages would get different results, the spec has not pinned the behavior and it should be flagged as a gap rather than enforced.

Flag dead checks — a check that emits FAILURE with no reachable SUCCESS counterpart or sits behind an always-false guard — and weak logic, such as a missing or malformed input that silently passes or an assertion that cannot distinguish rejected-for-the-right-reason from rejected-at-all.

A conformance PR must reference at least one real implementation the scenario ran green against — the in-repo everything-client/server or an external SDK via the pkg.pr.new preview build — and its negative test must pin the specific failing check slugs rather than merely assert that the failure count is greater than zero.

In a scenario review, order findings spec-backing then logic/dead then coverage then conventions, present each finding as a self-contained bullet carrying the check id, a file:line permalink pinned to the PR head SHA, the quoted normative sentence, and the consequence, and keep spec gaps in a separate trailing list because they go upstream rather than to the PR author.
The MCP Inspector is an interactive developer tool for testing and debugging Model Context Protocol servers.
The MCP Inspector runs directly through npx and requires no separate installation step.
The Inspector is launched against a target server using the form `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector <command> [args...]`.

condition: the server is a local TypeScript build

The server connection pane selects the transport used to connect to the server and, for local servers, allows customizing the command-line arguments and environment.

The MCP Inspector is a developer tool for testing and debugging MCP servers, composed of two cooperating components: the MCP Inspector Client (MCPI), a React-based web UI, and the MCP Proxy (MCPP), a Node.js protocol-bridge server.

The MCP Proxy is a protocol bridge that acts simultaneously as an MCP client (connecting to the target server) and an HTTP server (serving the web UI); it is not a network proxy that intercepts traffic.
The proxy connects the browser-based UI to MCP servers over multiple transport methods: stdio, SSE, and streamable-http.
Running the MCP Inspector requires Node.js version ^22.7.5.
To inspect an MCP server implementation there is no need to clone the inspector repository; it is run via npx (npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector).

When launching a target server through the inspector, arguments are passed directly to the server, environment variables are set with the -e flag, and a `--` separator is used to distinguish inspector flags from server arguments.
The Inspector serves the MCPI client UI on default port 6274 and the MCPP proxy server on default port 6277, both overridable via the CLIENT_PORT and SERVER_PORT environment variables.
Because the proxy server can spawn local processes and connect to any specified MCP server, it must not be exposed to untrusted networks.
The proxy server requires authentication by default: a random session token is generated at startup and must be supplied as a Bearer token in the Authorization header on every request to the server.

Disabling proxy authentication via DANGEROUSLY_OMIT_AUTH is strongly discouraged because it exposes the host to browser-based remote compromise — a malicious website or advertisement can attack the machine — a risk tracked as CVE-2025-49596.
condition: when proxy authentication is disabled

statement: The proxy authentication token can be supplied non-interactively by setting the MCP_PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN environment variable (for example a value from openssl rand -hex 32).
By default both the proxy server and the client bind only to localhost to prevent network access; binding to all interfaces via HOST=0.0.0.0 should be done only in trusted network environments.
condition: only in trusted network environments

statement: The Inspector mitigates DNS rebinding attacks by validating the Origin header, allowing only the client origin by default (respecting CLIENT_PORT, default 6274); additional origins are permitted via the comma-separated ALLOWED_ORIGINS environment variable.
The Inspector supports bearer-token authentication for SSE connections, sending the token in the Authorization header, with the header name overridable in the UI.
MCP_SERVER_REQUEST_TIMEOUT (default 300000 ms) is a client-side timeout: the Inspector cancels a request if no response is received within it, independently of any server-side timeout.

Inspector client-side timeouts and server-side timeouts are independent, whichever elapses first determines the resulting error; the Inspector timeout must therefore be set appropriately for elicitation or long-running operations.
MCP_REQUEST_MAX_TOTAL_TIMEOUT (default 60000 ms) caps the total time for requests sent to the MCP server and is intended for use with progress notifications.
MCP_AUTO_OPEN_ENABLED can only be set as an environment variable and is not configurable from within the browser.
The Inspector supports config files (--config <path> --server <name>) that store settings for multiple MCP servers, and it auto-detects each server's transport type from the config file.
The Inspector auto-selects a server without an explicit --server argument when the config contains a single server, or a server named 'default-server'.
condition: config contains a single server or one named default-server

statement: When both a query parameter and the corresponding localStorage item are set, the query parameter takes precedence.

The Servers File Export offers a 'Server Entry' button that copies a single server configuration for insertion into an existing mcp.json mcpServers object, and a 'Servers File' button that copies a complete mcp.json with the current server registered as 'default-server'.
CLI mode enables programmatic, scriptable interaction with MCP servers and is well suited to automation, CI/CD pipelines, and a rapid feedback loop with AI coding assistants.
CLI mode supports operations across tools, resources, and prompts via the --method flag, with tool arguments supplied as --tool-arg key=value pairs or as a JSON-encoded string.
In CLI mode a remote MCP server defaults to SSE transport; --transport http selects streamable HTTP and --header supplies custom request headers.
When building tool requests, optional fields with empty values should be omitted, unless the field's schema defines an explicit default that matches the current value.

statement: An explicit schema default (for example default: null) should be preserved in the request when the current value matches it, because it is a meaningful value the tool expects.
Required fields must always be included in a tool request even when their values are empty, so the MCP server can validate them and return appropriate error messages.
The Inspector client should perform only basic field-presence checking and defer deep parameter validation to the MCP server according to its schema.
In test watch mode, changes to test files are picked up automatically, but changes to CLI source are not reflected without a rebuild.
The CLI tests run in parallel across test files but sequentially within a single file.
Test config files are made unique for parallel execution using crypto.randomUUID(), and HTTP/SSE test servers use dynamic port allocation to avoid port conflicts.
Code coverage is not collected for the CLI test suite because much of the code under test runs in a spawned subprocess that Vitest cannot track.
The CLI test suite relies on built-in MCP test servers and has no external dependency on registry-hosted servers.
While Inspector V2 is under development, V1 contributions should be limited to bug fixes and MCP spec compliance.

MCP exposes three complementary debugging surfaces at different levels: the MCP Inspector, server-side logging, and client developer tools.

The MCP Inspector is an interactive, transport-agnostic testing UI that connects to stdio or Streamable HTTP servers and can invoke a server's tools, prompts, and resources while watching its notification stream.
The Inspector is the recommended first step when developing or diagnosing an MCP server.
