Running the SDK's snapshot-based MCP server test requires installing pytest and inline-snapshot (via pip or uv).
condition: to run the snapshot-style test shown in the docs

statement: In a FastMCP tool, the function's docstring is automatically used as the tool's description.
inline-snapshot lets you capture snapshots of test output, which makes writing MCP server tests easier and is promoted as a best practice, but it is optional.
exception: you do not need inline-snapshot; tests can be written without it

statement: Define a pytest fixture named anyio_backend that returns "asyncio" to select the async backend for MCP async tests.
exception: if the code uses trio instead of asyncio, return "trio" instead

statement: When using trio as the async backend, set the anyio_backend fixture to return "trio".
condition: the async code runs on trio rather than asyncio

statement: Expose the connected client session to tests via an async-generator pytest fixture that opens create_connected_server_and_client_session(app, ...) with async with and yields the session, so the context manager tears the session down after the test.

Mark asynchronous MCP test functions with @pytest.mark.anyio so pytest runs them under the configured anyio backend.
Invoke a server tool inside a test by awaiting client_session.call_tool(tool_name, arguments_dict), e.g. call_tool("add", {"a": 1, "b": 2}).

A tool call returns a CallToolResult whose content is a list of TextContent items (the text form) and whose structuredContent holds the machine-readable result; e.g. an integer result 3 appears as TextContent text "3" and structuredContent {"result": 3}.
Assert a tool-call result by comparing it against snapshot(CallToolResult(...)) from inline-snapshot, using snapshot testing to pin the expected content and structuredContent.

A Client follows a single lifecycle: construct it, enter it with `async with`, then call its async methods; every protocol verb (listing tools, calling one, reading a resource, rendering a prompt) is an async method that returns a typed result.
The `async with` block is the Client's entire lifecycle: entering it connects and negotiates the protocol and leaving it disconnects, so there is no separate connect()/close() pair to call.
A Client instance cannot be reused after its `async with` block has exited.
`Client` accepts one positional argument and resolves which transport to use from that argument's type.
Passing an `MCPServer` (or low-level `Server`) instance to `Client` connects in-process over the in-memory transport, with no subprocess, no port, and no HTTP.
condition: when Client's positional argument is an MCPServer or low-level Server instance

statement: Passing a URL string to `Client` connects over Streamable HTTP, the production transport path.
condition: when Client's positional argument is a URL string

statement: Passing a transport object (anything usable as `async with ... as (read, write)`, such as `stdio_client(...)` wrapping a subprocess) connects the Client over that transport.
condition: when Client's positional argument is a transport object

statement: Entering the block populates four read-only connection properties on the client: server_info, server_capabilities, protocol_version, and instructions.
`server_capabilities` reports what the server can do, and a capability the server does not have is exposed as `None`.
condition: the specific capability attribute is None when the server lacks that capability

statement: `client.instructions` holds the server's `instructions=` string, or `None` when the server set none.
condition: None when the server did not set instructions=

statement: You never pick a protocol version: by default the Client probes the server and falls back to the classic handshake for older servers, so one client works against any era of server.
condition: by default, unless you explicitly control the protocol version

statement: `client.session` exposes the underlying `ClientSession` as a low-level escape hatch that ordinary client code does not need.
`list_tools()` returns a `ListToolsResult` whose `.tools` holds each tool's complete definition: name, title, description, and input_schema.
`tool.input_schema` is the JSON Schema the server derives from the tool function's type hints.

Because a tool's `title` is optional, a UI must fall back to the tool `name` when no title is set; `get_display_name` from `mcp.shared.metadata_utils` performs this fallback for tools, resources, resource templates, and prompts.
condition: when a tool sets no title

statement: `call_tool(name, arguments)` runs the tool and returns a `CallToolResult` carrying three separately-consumed fields: content, structured_content, and is_error.

`content` is a list of content blocks, where a block is a union of TextContent, ImageContent, AudioContent, ResourceLink, or EmbeddedResource, and one tool may return several blocks of different kinds.

Narrow a content block with `isinstance(block, TextContent)` before reading `block.text`, because other block types (for example ImageContent) expose different attributes such as `.data`, and the type checker rejects `.text` outside the isinstance.
`structured_content` is the tool's return value as JSON matching the tool's declared output_schema, so application code needs no string parsing.
When both are present, `content` and `structured_content` deliberately carry the same information twice: content for a model to read and structured_content for application code.
condition: when both content and structured_content are present

statement: A tool that raises does not raise in the client; the failure returns as an ordinary result with `is_error=True`.
exception: the client raises MCPError only when the server replies with a JSON-RPC error instead of a result

statement: A raising tool's exception message is placed in `content` so the model can read it and retry, treating a tool error as part of the conversation rather than a crash.
Always inspect `is_error` before trusting `structured_content`.
When a tool call fails (`is_error=True`), `structured_content` is `None`.
condition: when is_error is True

statement: `is_error=True` also covers failures beyond your own raise: calling a tool the server does not have (for example `call_tool("does_not_exist", {})`) returns the same shape with is_error=True and an "Unknown tool" message in content, without raising.

`list_resources()` returns the concrete resources (those with a fixed URI) and `list_resource_templates()` returns the parameterised ones (URI templates); they are two separate lists because a template is not readable until its parameters are filled in.
`read_resource(uri)` takes a plain string URI and works on both concrete resources and filled-in templates, with the server matching a filled URI to its template.
`read_resource` returns `contents`, a list of TextResourceContents or BlobResourceContents; narrow each with `isinstance` before reading `.text` (or `.blob`).

On 2025-era connections a client is notified of resource changes via the `subscribe_resource`/`unsubscribe_resource` pair, which `MCPServer` does not implement, so on the 2026-07-28 wire (where those verbs no longer exist) such a request answers `-32601`, Method not found.
condition: on 2025-era connections; the subscribe_resource/unsubscribe_resource verbs are gone on the 2026-07-28 wire

statement: The 2026 replacement for resource subscription is a `subscriptions/listen` stream, which `MCPServer` does serve, so `server_capabilities.resources.subscribe` is `True` there.
condition: on the 2026 wire

statement: `list_prompts()` reports the prompts a server offers together with each prompt's name, title, and required arguments.
`get_prompt(name, arguments)` renders a prompt, and its arguments dict is always string-to-string because prompt arguments are always strings.
`get_prompt` returns `messages`, a list of PromptMessage each carrying a role and a content block, which a host hands straight to the model.

A server with a completion handler can autocomplete prompt and resource-template arguments as the user types via `client.complete(ref=..., argument=...)`, where `ref` is a PromptReference or ResourceTemplateReference and `argument` is `{name, value}` (the argument and what the user has typed); the suggestions come back in `result.completion.values`.
Every `list_*` method accepts a `cursor=` keyword and every result carries a `next_cursor`; page by looping — call with the cursor, collect the results, and stop when `next_cursor` is `None`.
`MCPServer` returns everything in a single page, so `next_cursor` is `None` and a pagination loop runs once; the same loop is still correct against servers that genuinely page.
condition: MCPServer returns one page; other servers may return more

statement: `Client(mcp)` with no process and no port is already a test harness for the server, and the in-memory transport it uses is the connection path every example and every test on this page relies on.

exception: the flag affects in-memory connections only

client.ping() accepts an optional timeout option expressed in milliseconds (e.g. { timeout: 5000 }).

The SDK assigns the progressToken automatically when the caller supplies an onprogress callback.
condition: the caller provides an onprogress callback on the request

statement: A progress update object carries a numeric progress field plus optional total and message fields.
Setting resetTimeoutOnProgress: true on a request resets that request's timeout each time a progress update is received.
condition: resetTimeoutOnProgress is enabled on the request

A progress notification's params must include the progressToken along with the current progress (and optionally total and message).
A server handler should send a progress notification only when extra._meta.progressToken is defined.
condition: the request supplied a progressToken

For unit and integration tests of MCP server logic, prefer wiring the client and server with InMemoryTransport.createLinkedPair(): it drives the real protocol path (initialize handshake, JSON-RPC framing, capability negotiation, tool/resource dispatch) with no socket or subprocess, keeping tests fast and deterministic.
condition: unit/integration testing of MCP server logic
exception: for end-to-end transport-level tests, use stdio or Streamable-HTTP instead

statement: Reserve stdio or Streamable-HTTP transports for end-to-end, transport-level tests rather than for unit tests of server logic.
condition: end-to-end, transport-level testing

statement: InMemoryTransport connects a Client and an McpServer within a single process, using no sockets, subprocess, or HTTP.
InMemoryTransport.createLinkedPair() is a static factory that returns a two-element tuple [clientTransport, serverTransport].
Each transport from a linked pair holds a private reference to its peer, so a send() on one is delivered directly to the peer's onmessage handler with no serialization boundary or network hop.
Messages sent before the peer attaches its onmessage handler are queued and flushed on start(), so the order in which the two connect() calls run is not fragile.
Calling close() on either linked transport tears down both ends and fires onclose.
A single transport.close() in test teardown is sufficient; the linked transports do not need to be closed separately.
condition: in test teardown

statement: InMemoryTransport.send() takes an optional authInfo option, enabling tests to exercise authenticated or authInfo-dependent server handlers in-process.
InMemoryTransport is intended for testing and development; for production in-process connections the SDK directs users to StreamableHTTPClientTransport against a local server URL.
condition: in-process connection for testing/development
exception: for production in-process connections, use StreamableHTTPClientTransport against a local server URL

statement: The canonical in-memory wiring is to create a linked pair and then await Promise.all([client.connect(clientTransport), mcpServer.connect(serverTransport)]).
Both connect() calls must run concurrently (e.g. under Promise.all); connecting only one side, or awaiting the two connect() calls sequentially, deadlocks the initialize handshake.

mcp-validation validates MCP servers for protocol compliance, security, and correct implementation.

The tool's validation spans six aspects: the MCP initialize handshake and protocol compliance, JSON-RPC 2.0 conformance, capability testing of tools/prompts/resources, mcp-scan security analysis, registry-schema conformance, and JSON report generation.
The tool supports three transports and validates each: stdio (the default), HTTP, and SSE.
HTTP transport supports full OAuth 2.0 with three methods: automatic Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591), pre-registered client id/secret, and a personal access token.
SSE transport authenticates with a simple Bearer token.
The OAuth flow opens a browser automatically, runs a local callback server on localhost:3333, exchanges tokens using PKCE, and times out user authentication after 5 minutes.
Security analysis is performed by integrating mcp-scan to scan the server's tools for vulnerabilities.
Pass --skip-mcp-scan to skip the mcp-scan security analysis for faster validation.
condition: when faster validation is wanted and security analysis is not required

statement: The process exits 0 when the server is MCP-compliant and 1 when validation fails, giving CI/CD pipelines a machine-readable pass/fail signal.

The validation pipeline runs in a fixed order: start the server process, send the initialize request, check JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol compliance, discover capabilities, run the (optional) mcp-scan security analysis, then generate the JSON report.
For stdio servers, place the server command after a `--` separator so the server's own flags are not consumed by mcp-validate (needed e.g. for npx packages).
condition: stdio transport where the server command carries its own flags

statement: MCP servers can be validated through a container runtime such as podman or docker, e.g. `podman run -i --rm <image>`.
HTTP and SSE transports require the server endpoint URL to be supplied via --endpoint.
condition: http or sse transport

statement: Server environment variables are supplied with the repeatable --env KEY=VALUE flag.
Override the global validation timeout with --timeout when a server is slow to start or respond.
condition: default timeout too short for the server

statement: Use --json-report FILE to export a detailed JSON validation report, e.g. to upload as a CI artifact.
Validation behaviour is selected with --profile, individual validators are toggled with --enable/--disable, and --list-profiles / --list-validators enumerate the available options.
The --repo-url option validates a server's repository for open-source-compliance.
The --debug option emits execution context (working directory, Python version, platform), full command details, environment variables, process lifecycle events, and per-validator timing and results.
Sensitive environment-variable values are masked in the tool's debug output (for example API_KEY is shown as ab*****ef).
A programmatic API (validate_mcp_server_command / validate_server) returns a result or session exposing is_valid / overall_success, the errors list, discovered tools, and capabilities.
The framework is plugin-based: each validation type is a separate, independently configurable validator plugin.
Validators declare dependencies on one another and are executed in dependency order.
Validation profiles are pre-configured suites of validators for a use case, and their settings can be overridden at runtime via CLI flags, environment variables, or a config file.

The built-in profiles map to use cases: `basic` (protocol + capabilities) for quick dev/CI checks, `comprehensive` (protocol, capabilities, ping, errors, security) as the thorough default, `security_focused` (protocol, strict errors, required security) for audits, and `development` (protocol, capabilities, ping, errors, continue-on-failure) for local debugging.
`protocol` is the required foundation validator — it checks the initialize handshake, protocol version, and server info — and every other validator depends on it.

Beyond protocol the built-in validators are `capabilities` (tools/prompts/resources lists), `ping` (ping round-trip and response time), `errors` (JSON-RPC invalid-method and malformed-request handling), and `security` (mcp-scan), each depending on protocol.
A .mcp-validation.json config file defines named profiles with global_timeout, continue_on_failure, and per-validator enabled / required / parameters settings.
Validation can be configured through environment variables MCP_VALIDATION_CONFIG (config file path) and MCP_VALIDATION_PROFILE (active profile name).

Validators expose tuning parameters, such as protocol strict_version_check, ping max_response_time_ms, errors strict_error_codes / test_malformed_requests, and security run_mcp_scan / vulnerability_threshold / save_scan_results.
When mcp-scan is not found, install it (for example `uvx install mcp-scan`) or disable the security validator.
condition: mcp-scan is unavailable on the host

statement: Run the mcp-validate tool inside its dedicated virtual environment via `uv run`.

To register servers, clone each server's repository into a tmp_servers folder at the project root.
Derive server metadata from the cloned README: a uuid id, the original server name, a short description, and repository fields (url, source set to github, and the numeric GitHub repository id).
Set version_detail.version to the tag after the last ':' in the container image reference, release_date to today, and is_latest to true.
Represent packages as a single docker entry with registry_name docker, name set to the image without its version tag, version set to the tag, plus environment_variables and package_arguments.
Extract environment-variable names exactly as documented in the README (for example from `-e VARIABLE_NAME` Docker examples); never assume, invent, or standardize variable names.

For each environment variable record name, description, is_required, default, is_secret, and choices, omitting is_required / default / choices when uncertain and marking usernames and sensitive values as is_secret.
exception: a field's value is uncertain, in which case omit it

A validation can succeed while still emitting warnings: in the sample run all 7 servers succeeded with 0 errors but 21 total warnings.

Recurring warning categories observed in practice are container images not based on UBI, mcp-scan security analysis failing with 'NoneType' errors, and JSON-RPC error-compliance issues on invalid-method / malformed-request handling.
Servers that lack a containerized (Docker) distribution cannot be validated by this container-based flow and were skipped.
condition: the server has no containerized distribution
